subsubtopic: CHILDREN LIVING IN POVERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the latest statistics from the National Council of Welfare illustrate the tragedy of the children of Canada, more than one million of whom are living in poverty. Almost four million Canadians are living in poverty. Yet, to read an interview given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) in Faith Today entitled "Saints in Caesar's Household", you would think that people living in poverty choose their lot in life. He says:
We have to recognize that there are those who are poor because of circumstances, but many by their own decisions are where they are.
Are those million children living in poverty where they are by choice? When the Minister was questioned on this issue earlier this week in committee he suggested that abusing families are also there by their own decision. It seems to me that when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) expresses this kind of attitude in a magazine he should be giving some answers to Canadian people.
The one million Canadian children are not living in poverty by choice. Abusing families are not abusing by choice. There is in fact work which must be done in this area. I frankly hang my head in shame when the Canadian Minister of National Health and Welfare makes a statement like that in a magazine in which he is labeled a saint in Caesar's household.

subsubtopic: LOW-LEVEL TRAINING FLIGHTS OVER LABRADOR-ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REVIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last fall the Government announced an environmental impact hearing on the proposal to build a NATO base at Goose Bay, Labrador. These hearings were scheduled to evaluate the legitimacy of the complaints that low-level flights would have destructive impacts on the environment and the Innu people of Labrador.
In January the Federal Environmental Assessment Review Panel issued interim recommendations that the number of low-level flights not be increased so that no further damage would be done to the environment or to the Innu people prior to the review being completed.
This week, according to news reports, the Department of National Defence showed its contempt for the FEARO process by rejecting that interim recommendation and by having the Minister sign an agreement with the Netherlands Air Force to engage in low-level flight training with the Dutch which will add 10 to 16 aircraft and a great number of daily or weekly flights.
I call upon the Government to stop using environmental hearings as mere public relations gestures, to take seriously the needs of the Innu people, and to stop breaking faith with the Canadian public.

subsubtopic: OUTBREAK OF FOREST FIRES-CAMPERS URGED TO EXERCISE CAUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a very serious problem has developed very rapidly in the forests of western and northern Canada. They are tinder dry at this moment and, as I speak, thousands of acres are raging under forest fires, posing a serious problem to all Canadians.
We have already lost $100 million in forests. In Manitoba alone there are 400 people fighting forest fires. Fifty homes in Fisher Bay had to be evacuated and at Wallace Lake there is another extremely serious fire.
This is the first long weekend when thousands of Canadians will go to the forests to enjoy camping. I ask the Government and all Members of Parliament to urge everyone to exercise extreme caution when setting campfires because most fires are caused by human error and carelessness.
I am sure that if it does not rain in western Canada we will lose many more hundreds of thousands of acres of our forests. This is an important concern, and everyone should be very much aware of the importance of our forests.

speechtext:

We share the sentiments expressed yesterday by the Prime Minister of New Zealand who told his House of Representatives: "That the parliamentary democracy which was so recently reinforced in Fiji by the general election should have gone in such a way is abhorrent".
All Members of the House will be concerned about the subversion of democracy anywhere. That such subversion by

the military should take place in the Parliament of a sister commonwealth country is especially distressing.

subtopic: EFFECT OF FORMER NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
EFFECT OF FORMER NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Ralph Hedlin writes in the Western Report magazine, and I quote:
It will soon be seven years since Pierre Trudeau's Government laid down a new set of principles to govern western oil and gas policy-the National Energy Program of October 28, 1980.
The National Energy Program was the capstone of a decade of intense Trudeau Liberal Government intervention in oil and gas during the years of 1974-84.
The Trudeau Liberals, among whom John Turner was a major player, put in position policies that transferred a greedy proportion of the benefits from the west to the consumers of central Canada and the tax-gatherers in Ottawa.
Every year new evidences surface that bear witness to the damage done by the intervention of the federal politicians and bureaucrats.
The most recent is the demise of Dome Petroleum. The wild irresponsibility of the debt accumulation of the Trudeau years is only comprehensible if one accepts that the Government was satisfied it could recover by looting the west of revenues produced by $100 oil. Interest charges on those immense debts are a major contributor to today's deficits and a major drag on the Mulroney Government.
In the long history of Canada there has been no economic initiative that has been as utterly wrong-headed and as disastrously damaging as the energy policies of the Trudeau years. It is a root cause of much of the economic frailty and regional distrust in Canada.
The players have passed from the stage, nearly, but we are still suffering the legacy of those policies from those years.

May 15, 1987

Mr. Speaker, recently a 14-year-old girl was refused an abortion at Royal Inland Hospital in Kamloops. She was forced to suffer a very difficult forced delivery which will scar her emotionally for the rest of her life. Across British Columbia women's access to abortion is becoming more and more restricted as politicians, led by the Premier, are imposing their personal moral views on women despite the fact that the general public supports greater access to abortion under our existing legislation.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO MEMBERS OF POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Police Week was established as a means by which this nation could officially recognize and pay tribute to those men and women who have chosen a career to protect and serve their communities. I am pleased to have the opportunity to express my personal views, my profound respect and heartfelt appreciation for these men and women.
Police work requires a special kind of person. They must have courage to deal with the dangers inherent in their work. They must be fair and impartial in enforcing the law. They must have integrity beyond reproach. They must exhibit and utilize consideration, sensitivity and compassion when dealing with the public. Those personal characteristics have always been, and are still required by police officers.
However, new skills have been incorporated into modern-day policing. The police officer today requires many of the skills of a psychologist, social worker, criminologist, computer scientist, lawyer, accountant and administrator. Police forces have in recent years moved rapidly to adjust to these new demands and have developed and engaged officers to meet the challenge of crime in today's society.
I believe all Members of this House will join in paying tribute to these police officers and to the Chiefs of Police
across this nation who have meet these new challenges with resolve and are serving each and every Canadian as they fulfil their responsibilities on behalf of us all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak about Unemployment Insurance.
Since its inception over 40 years ago, unemployment insurance has evolved into one of our most important national programs, touching almost every Canadian and forming an important element of Canada's economy. Originally, unemployment insurance was meant to provide temporary income protection against an unexpected job loss. Over the years, it also became a response to seasonal unemployment. Today, for many, it remains temporary income protection. For others, it has become a frequently used source of guaranteed income. For others it provides what are called "social benefits" such as income support during maternity leave.

Few government programs affect so many people in Canada. This was never clearer than during the recession of the early 1980s when, out of necessity, more and more people from all walks of life turned to unemployment insurance for support. Such an important and broad program having such an important effect on so many individuals, economic sectors, and regions of the country was naturally prone to criticism from different quarters for different reasons.

When we came into office, Mr. Speaker, we decided that the Unemployment Insurance program needed to be reviewed. We had to ensure that it continued to meet the needs of Canadians. We established a Commission of Inquiry to examine the program and its place in the Canadian economy. We asked that, for the first time, there be public hearings across the country to receive the views of all interested Canadians.
In December we received the Report of that Commission, which included a minority report by two commissioners and supplementary statements by four commissioners. In the past six months the Government has considered carefully the advice of all of the commissioners. As well we have studied the recommendations of the Royal Commission in Newfoundland, the Macdonald Commission recommendations and those of the Standing Committee.
Members of this House will know that there are sharp and irreconcilable differences between these studies.
The Government has listened closely to the public debate. We have consulted widely on the subject. I have met with worker and employer groups. I have received representations from many Canadians, who have made their views known to me. These consultations made it clear that opinion on Unemployment Insurance is divided-even polarized. Some want a more generous unemployment insurance system while others want a more restrictive program.

May 15, 1987
Statement by Ministers
I have also met twice with the provinces on the Unemployment Insurance Program. Some provinces are strongly opposed to any move to a more restrictive program, while others want the social aspects to be removed. Mr. Speaker, two distinct schools of thought have emerged. One school holds that to achieve the objectives of the current program, it should be broken apart into at least two distinct programs: insurance on one side and what are called social benefits on the other. It is argued that the current system actually encourages people not to work-that unemployment insurance should return to strict insurance principles and let the social benefits be handled by another, unspecified, mechanism.
The other school of thought holds that the scope and coverage of unemployment insurance should be expanded and enriched. It is proposed that unemployment insurance play a stronger income support role. This school rejects as "myth" the notion that substantial numbers of Canadians draw unemployment insurance in preference to holding a job. Thus the proposals are for more money to be introduced into the program. The distinction between social benefits and insurance principles is simply not accepted.
Each of these schools is not only sharply critical of the other, but each forecasts disastrous results if the other's proposals are implemented. But everyone is agreed that any change in the design of the program would profoundly affect millions of individuals and the economies of the regions where they live.
The Government has considered carefully the current program and all of the proposals for a change in its design. We reject the argument that unemployment insurance benefits should be expanded and enriched. Not only would this be expensive and require an increase of premium payments by all Canadians, it may well create disincentives to work.
Equally, we reject the proposals for a reduction of unemployment insurance benefits. Such reductions would hurt blameless individuals and would damage the economies of certain regions of the country.
As the Government charged with representing an interest of all Canadians, we have concluded that the competing and conflicting opinions of all the interested parties are, at best, reconciled within the current structure of unemployment insurance.
The common element in all the proposals for change is that they would cause hardship among individuals, businesses, and regions, all for an uncertain result. This would be counterproductive to the progress we have made in rebuilding our economy, supporting regional development, and creating jobs.

The Government acknowledges unemployment insurance is not a perfect program, but the current system is helping millions of Canadians and we will not induce unnecessary
uncertainty by attempting change for the sake of change. Our plan is not to reduce unemployment insurance but to reduce the need for unemployment insurance.

We must continue to do what helps Canada achieve durable employment. All our economic, fiscal and regional development, trade and human resource development policies are dedicated to this end. Unemployment insurance is assisting in those efforts and will continue to do so.
Unemployment insurance is only one tool within the package of our labour market and employment development programs. The Canadian Jobs Strategy plays a vital role in assisting Canadians to adjust to changing economic circumstances.
While the employment picture is steadily improving- 778,000 jobs have been created since September, 1984-and we have an excellent and effective set of programs, I cannot and shall not rest complacent. I intend to ensure that the jobs strategy remains responsive to regional needs and labour market changes, responsive to the needs of individuals such as women re-entering the workforce, the older unemployed, youth making the transition from school to work, those workers facing shifts in global trading pattern, and technological change, and the long-term unemployed.
Reducing regional disparity is a major goal of the Government. We are giving special emphasis to diversifying the economic base of western Canada. We have taken steps to assist the oil industry and we are working to help the agricultural sector. The Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will improve federal development initiatives in Atlantic Canada.
Throughout my consideration of unemployment insurance, I have been struck by the importance of how the unemployment insurance program is administered. For most people, the way the program is delivered is the first issue raised. Our staff in the Canada Employment Centres do a fine job in what are often difficult circumstances, but I believe that we can and must do better in administering the program. We can provide better and mQre sensitive service to our clients and we can better control abuse by those who would cheat the unemployment insurance program.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to outline administrative initiatives which we will implement, and which should be fully operational in 1988.
We will place Claimant Services Officers in our busiest offices. These people will work directly with our claimants to provide clear explanations and help when it is needed. We will provide public awareness sessions, so people can understand the system, and will know what to expect. We will provide better telephone access so our clients can be spared the frustration of busy phone lines, and can get the information they need about their claims.
May 15, 1987

We will implement a simplified Record of Employment after consultations with employers and employees to reduce the paper burden on employers.
We will step up our activities to weed out those who would abuse the system. There will be enhanced job search and availability interviews. We will serve our claimants better- those honest people who would rather work than collect unemployment insurance. The small group who would cheat the Unemployment Insurance Program, and who tarnish the reputation of all claimants, will not be tolerated.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to thank each member of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration for their work on the Unemployment Insurance Program.
Their report was most helpful in our consideration of not only the current program but the other proposals for reform we received. The committee suggested we consider its recommendations as a package and we have done so.
1 am tabling today a letter to the Chairman of the Standing Committee reflecting the contents of my statement which will serve as the Government's response to the Report in accordance with the Standing Orders.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, Canadians are laughing at the Government this morning but they are not amused. After two and a half years and millions of dollars spent on four commissions and studies, the Forget Commission, the Macdonald Commission, the Newfoundland Royal Commission and the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, the Minister comes to the House this morning and says he is going to do absolutely nothing about unemployment insurance reform. There will be no Bill dealing with necessary reform of the Unemployment Insurance Act. The Minister mentioned a few administrative changes which he could have put in place two years or three years ago without any study whatsoever.
On November 8, 1984, the Minister of Finance in his Economic Statement said:
To ensure that this program-
The Unemployment Insurance Program.
-meets the needs of individuals in adjusting to rapidly changing labour market conditions at a reasonable cost to workers, employers and the Government, statutory changes are likely to be required. Accordingly, the Government has initiated a review of the Unemployment Insurance program to be undertaken on an urgent basis. A discussion paper will be published shortly by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) followed by appropriate parliamentary review.
The Minister then went on to give us more details in his book entitled A New Direction for Canada. An Agenda for Economic Renewal. Talk about urgency. The Government then took seven months to set up the Forget Commission which cost this country nearly $7 million. After more than a year and
Statement by Ministers
a half of research and study and hearings, Forget produced his report in December of 1986, along with two minority reports. The commission was very severely divided.
At that time we in the Liberal Party took strong exception to proposals by Forget to reduce benefits by a method of calculating them on the basis of annualization, and to his proposals to cut seasonal and regional benefits. The Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration then undertook a study of the Forget Report and made its own report on the subject in March of 1987. The committee unanimously rejected the annualization proposal and cuts in benefits and made 90 recommendations for improvement to the Unemployment Insurance Program. Many of these recommendations were similar to the Forget Commission's recommendations. There were agreements between the standing committee and the Forget Commission on some essential points.
The Minister, however, has ignored all these proposals. He has done nothing to extend unemployment insurance to the growing number of part-time workers. He has done nothing to improve maternity and parental benefits. He has done nothing to provide more training opportunities for those on unemployment insurance. He has done nothing to clarify the law with respect to those locked out or unable to work during strikes. He has done nothing to bring equity to the problem of overpayments.
During our hearings we heard many horror stories of people who were paid the wrong amount of unemployment insurance benefits. It was through no fault of their own but was the fault of government officials. Yet they were asked to pay back thousands of dollars while they were still unemployed. Nothing is going to be done about that. The Minister has said nothing about the restructuring of the Unemployment Insurance Commission to make it more efficient and independent.
The Government is once again abandoning its political agenda. Once again it has ignored a unanimous committee report, despite great claims for parliamentary reform.

Mr. Speaker, this Government brought in parliamentary reform, but this month it managed to ignore two unanimous reports from the Committee on Employment and Immigration, one on refugees and one on unemployment insurance.

Twice in one month the Government, which has prided itself on Parliamentary reform, has ignored two unanimous committee reports from the same committee. The Minister's claim in his statement that "Our plan is not to reduce unemployment insurance but to reduce the need for unemployment insurance" is a real farce. If the Minister has in mind some new programs to combat unemployment, where are they? He certainly did not announce them this morning.
The rate of unemployment in this country is still 9.3 per cent with 1.2 million persons out of work. We have not yet returned

May 15, 1987
Statement by Ministers
to the pre-recession rate of 7.5 per cent unemployment which existed in 1981 and we are three years out of the recession. We have nowhere approached the average rate of unemployment of 5.6 per cent which existed in this country from 1965 to 1980. In fact, the Government has cut the employment and training programs by 30 per cent, from $2.2 billion in 1984 to $1.6 billion in this fiscal year. The Government's approach is one of laissez-faire resulting in low unemployment figures in the Toronto area but a 20 per cent rate in Newfoundland, a 12.6 per cent rate in British Columbia, a 10 per cent rate in Alberta and a 14 per cent rate for youth in this country.
The Government is doing nothing with respect to the growing number of low-paying, non-union part time jobs which have no benefits, 70 per cent of which are held by women. Nothing is being done about the growing gap between the incomes of men and women. This year for the first time in 18 years the gap widened rather than narrowed. The Government is also doing nothing about the growing gap between rich and poor as a result of the growing tendency to low paying parttime jobs.
The Unemployment Insurance Act was introduced by a Liberal Government in 1940 following the unemployment tragedy of the 1930s, The legislation was a great accomplishment of the Liberal Party under MacKenzie King. Over the years the Liberal Party has continued to refine, reform and fine tune the legislation. We still favour reform and improvement. We supported all the 90 recommendations in the standing committee report but one.
Much could have been done by the Government without touching controversial issues, but it has shown absolutely no leadership. The statement by the Minister today will not please anyone. It is a complete abdication of responsibility.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT RESPONSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, 1 want to express to the Minister my thanks for the promptness with which I received his statement. He said I would receive it in my office shortly after 9 a.m. and it was there shortly after 9 a.m. That is certainly an example which should be emulated by every Minister on the benches opposite.
Having said that, and that is the only one nice thing I am going to say about the Minister today, I do not think Canadians are laughing. I think that at 12.08 p.m. today, a collective sigh of relief went up from all the unemployed Canadians across this country. They are relieved because the Minister did not implement any of the Draconian recommendations of the Forget Commission. In fact, the Standing Committee of the House of Commons on Labour, Employment and Immigration is largely responsible for getting the Minister off the hook. He should get down on his knees and thank every single member of that standing committee of the House of Commons.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, May 15, 1987 is a great day for the rights of Canadian workers, who will keep unemployment insurance as a form of income support when looking for a job. It is probably
a slap in the face for Mr. Forget and his recommendation for annualization.
Members of the Standing Committee managed to put their personal views aside and unanimously recommended a set of measures and some thorough reforms for unemployment insurance. Members of all Parties in this House made it possible for the Government to save face and reject the abomination of annualization. Much remains to be done, however, to gain acceptance for measures that will improve the unemployment insurance system.
It is too bad that the Minister could not summon up his courage. As I read his statement I felt like a mosquito in a nudist colony-I just did not know where to begin.
First, I should set out very clearly that the only good thing that I can see in the statement is the fact that the recommendations of Forget have not been implemented. It is too bad that the Minister preferred to do this balancing act. As a matter of fact, I am surprised that he has been sitting on the fence for five months and 10 days from December 5 to May 15. It is five months and 10 days since the report of Forget was tabled in the House. The Minister sat on the fence for that length of time. I am surprised that today he is still on the fence and that there are not any splinters in his derri'ere. For five months and 10 days the Minister has been sitting on this egg. He was sitting on this egg, clucking and clucking, and what we have today in his statement is a scrambled result.
The Minister could not find the courage to deal with the unemployment insurance program in the positive way that was recommended by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. In his statement the Minister mentioned the Macdonald Commission Report, the report of the Newfoundland Royal Commission and the report of the committee of the House of Commons as if all three are separate reports. In fact, the Forget Commission Report was set up to study the recommendations of the Macdonald Commission. The standing committee of the House examined the Forget Report.
In the standing committee there sat members from all three Parties dominated by Conservatives. We considered Forget's report. We heard witnesses. In fact, the committee came back with 90 recommendations, 89 of them unanimous. Yet what has the Minister done instead of taking some of our recommendations? We recommended 10 weeks and 50 weeks of benefit. Yet what did we get? We got five and ten-five months and ten days that the Minister has been sitting on this issue.
We expected the Minister to deal with some of the positive recommendations we made. Some of the recommendations were with respect to maternity benefits. There was agreement from 99.99 per cent of the witnesses we heard that maternity benefits ought to be enhanced.
May 15, 1987

One of the most serious problems starting to emerge in our economy is with respect to part-time workers who are not only mostly women but young people. We looked at the question and we made a positive recommendation to the Government. Yet there has been no response to it.
We considered training, which was one of the issues in the Forget Commission Report. We specifically recommended to the Government certain items with respect to training. We did the same thing with respect to administration. In our report there are specific recommendations with respect to improving the records of employment so that delays to claimants can be avoided. So what will the Minister do with records of employment? He is going to consult. He is going to consult employers and employees. He is going to do more studies when there was a specific recommendation dealing with records of employment.
As for administration and local offices, we will improve the profits of Bell Telephone. A few more telephone lines will be put in. Does it take the $6 million or $7 million of taxpayers' money which was spent on Forget, the thousands of dollars which were spent on the expenses of the standing committee which studied Forget and five months and 10 days to discover that we do not have enough telephones in local offices? Has it taken that long for the Minister to discover that claimants are getting busy signals?
The Minister has set up a great straw person. Oh, there is abuse in the system, he says. We thoroughly examined the UI Program and all the evidence from the Minister's bureaucracy. The Minister clearly indicated that abuse in the system is 3 per cent or less. That compares with doctors in the medicare system. It compares with lawyers in the legal aid system. Three per cent abuse and the Minister says that we are going to cuff them with respect to benefit control to claimants.
We made specific recommendations with respect to how to deliver the services to legitimate claimants in an effective and efficient manner with as little delay as possible. The Minister has those recommendations in the report of the standing committee. Yet what does he do? He completely ignores the report and goes off to say, "Oh, well, we are going to consult with employers and employees to improve that. We are going to do this and do that".
We have entered into a new era with respect to standing committees of the House. They are supposed to have more power. They are supposed to participate more fully in what goes on and what should come from government. Well, our committee unanimously supported 89 recommendations. One recommendation, the ninetieth, was a majority recommendation. The Government has chosen to ignore these recommendations.
Ours was the first report on unemployment insurance that I have ever seen around here in which there was unanimity. Conservatives, who share the same ideology as the Minister, and some of them come from the same region as he, sat and discussed Forget with us. We called witnesses. We called
Petitions
Forget twice, and we called the members of his commission twice. We called the members of his commission who wrote the minority report. We talked to the bureaucrats. We talked to the Advisory Council on Employment and Immigration. The committee meetings were extensive. The Minister has a blueprint. Yet all the recommendations he picked out of the 90 amounted to zilch-zero. It is shameful that the Minister would ignore completely an arm of this House in the form of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration and not recognize the work it has done by implementing its recommendations which are positive and which enhance the Unemployment Insurance Program. It is indeed sad that it took the Minister five months and 10 days to come up with his statement.

subsubtopic: CANADA POST-OPPOSITION TO CORPORATE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have here several hundred petitions from various parts of Canada, including Repentigny, Rigaud and Ville Saint-Laurent, in the Province of Quebec, as well as Weston, in Ontario, i also have many petitions covered with the signatures of hundreds of residents of Belleville, in Ontario.
The petitioners feel that the new Canada Post corporate plan will create two classes of citizens through the permanent installation of superboxes in both urban and rural areas; that the closing of post offices in rural areas will deprive the citizens of a unique federal presence and reduce the level of postal service which is vital to rural communities; and that the rate increases, especially for second class mail, will jeopardize the distribution of many newspapers, regional weeklies, magazines and religious publications.
They humbly pray and call upon Parliament to turn down the Canada Post Corporate plan and urge Canada Post to deliver mail indiscriminately to all Canadian taxpayers.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS ON AUTO PACT SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have close to 1,300 names on three petitions dealing with the Auto Pact. The petitioners are resident in various parts of my constituency.
The first petition contains a total of 441 names, with the petitioners in this particular case coming mainly from the City of Windsor itself; the second petition, with 232 names, is from auto workers in the rural areas of the constituency; and the third petition contains the names of residents of many of the small towns throughout my constituency, such as Amherst-burg, Essex, Belle River, Stoney Point, and La Salle.
These petitions, as a whole, say to the Government that there is a great deal of concern that the safeguards built into the Auto Pact will be given away in the free trade talks with the United States. The petitioners call upon the Government to prevent any threat to the Canadian content safeguards of the Auto Pact and to maintain the promise that the Auto Pact will not be a subject for negotiation in the free trade talks with the United States.

subsubtopic: LOW-LEVEL FLIGHTS AT ARMED FORCES BASE AT GOOSE BAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition, duly certified by the Clerk of Petitions,
from a number of Canadian residents, from such places as Halifax, Sackville, Toronto, Cooper Creek, B.C., Hamilton, Winnipeg, Wolfville, Victoria, and Cote des Neiges.
These petitioners point out that the low-level flight training of pilots of NATO countries at the Canadian Forces Base at Goose Bay, Labrador disrupts the way of life of many of the native people in that area, and that it is also an aggressive and war-fighting action which tends to endanger world peace. They therefore ask Parliament to ensure that the Prime Minister ends all low-level flight training at Goose Bay Canadian Forces Base and ceases negotiating with NATO for the establishment of a larger base at that location.

subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARING BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Next I have a petition from some 150 Canadians, from such places as Saskatoon, Whitby, Grand Falls, St. John's, Newfoundland, Ottawa, Amherst-burg, Varennes, Quebec, Scarborough, St. Bruno, Charles-bourg, Hamilton, Montreal, Toronto, Mississauga, Estevan, Swift Current, Neville and Regina in Saskatchewan.
This petition points out that many people around the world are being forced to seek safety from persecution by coming to Canada. It goes on to point out that we have in the past in Canada had a good system for refugee determination but that system has now broken down.
There has been a proposal put forward, with support from all sides of this House, as well as from the Canadian Council of Churches, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Jewish Congress, and other groups, that Parliament should enact legislation that will embody the principles of fair and quick oral hearings for refugee claimants before a refugee board, independent of the Immigration Commission, and that there be provided universal access to these hearings for every claimant in Canada and adequate opportunity to arrive in Canada to make the claim that one is a refugee.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S O. 82- THE ENVIRONMENT- REQUEST THAT THE GOVERNMENT ENDORSE, ADOPT AND ADVOCATE, AT HOME AND ABROAD, THE GOALS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE BRUNDTLAND REPORT
speechtext:
-That this House urge the Government to endorse, adopt and advocate, at home and abroad, the goals and recommendations of the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development (Brundtland Report), entitled "Our Common Future";
That this report, dealing with global concerns, challenges and endeavours, be adopted as the central policy of the federal Government, its agencies and commissions; and
That the Minister of the Environment advocate the spirit and the substance of this report at the coming General Assembly of the United Nations on behalf of Canadians and of the global community, thus continuing Canada's tradition of giving leadership on environmental matters.
He said: Mr. Speaker, through this motion we urge the Government of Canadato endorse, adopt and advocate, at home and abroad, the goals and recommendations of the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development-
-widely known as the Brundtland Commission whose report is entitled "Our Common Future".
We are asking:
That this report, dealing with global concerns, challenges and endeavours, be adopted as the central policy of the federal Government, its agencies and commissions.
And finally, Mr. Speaker, we insist:
That the Minister of the Environment advocate the spirit and the substance of this report at the coming General Assembly of the United Nations on behalf of Canadians and of the global community, thus continuing Canada's tradition of giving leadership on environmental matters.
May 15, 1987



The history of the report goes back a few years to when the global community came to the conclusion that the environment and its protection and the understandable aspirations of developing nations had to be examined at the same time by way of a global commission. The debate was long and difficult. Finally, in December, 1983, the General Assembly gave the green light to the commission which came down with the report that we are discussing and debating today.
Canada's role or involvement in the time leading to the decision in December, 1983 was central, important, and of considerable significance, because of the role which Canada played in preceding years in other initiatives such as the discussions and negotiations leading to the adoption by the United Nations of the Law of the Sea.
In 1983, the then environment critic of the Official Opposition, who is now the Speaker, lent his support to the initiative. It is important to make that point because there has been, therefore, strong parliamentary support in addition to the government initiative at that time for what we are debating today.
What we are debating today is only one step in a long series of steps behind us and a number of important steps still ahead of us. The commission consisted of 22 individuals drawn from many regions of the globe. Among them were two Canadians. One was Maurice Strong who was very well known for the fact, among other things, that he was the Executive Director of UNEP and as Secretary General was the person in charge of the Stockholm environmental conference in 1972. The other Canadian was the Secretary General of the commission itself, Jim MacNeill. Preceding that assignment, he was the Director of Environment of the OECD. We can see that there was also participation in terms of human resources in the work of the commission by Canada, which lends additional significance and dimension to the report.
The report was released in London on April 27 of this year. I am glad that only 19 days later we have the opportunity in this House to debate its contents and to advance the cause embodied in the report entitled Our Common Future.
The commissioners advanced the debate on the environment from a theme of protection to a theme of survival of the human species on this planet, involving not only us as the human species, but the totality of living beings, with the background notion that between now and the year 2025 the population of this planet will double to almost nine billion persons. Given that today's population of 4.5 billion already has a substantial impact upon the environment, one can imagine the impact upon the resources of this globe if the population doubles and if we do not take certain precautions.
Therefore, the commissioners viewed the environment not only in the context of another public interest competing with existing interests, such as transport, finance, industry, agriculture, forestry, and the like, they stressed the importance of our capacity for a sustainable economy. In other words, they
Supply
stressed the importance of careful management of the natural resources available on earth and the immense impact upon natural resources being implemented in a manner which would ensure the regenerative capacity of nature.
It was in this sense that the words "sustainable development" suddenly emerged. These two words imply and require a longer definition, which I have just attempted to give, namely, to ensure that the regenerative capacity of nature is assured in order to provide sustainment and a capacity to draw from our natural resources-from fish, forests, water, soil, and air-in a manner which accommodates a population that is expected to double. In a nutshell, that is what sustainable development is all about. Therefore, it becomes a concept or almost a precondition for our approach to the business of Governments and to the public interest in years ahead.
In this scenario, for instance, the Minister of Finance becomes an agent for the environment, as do his colleagues such as the Ministers of Transport, Energy, Mines and Resources, Industry, Agriculture, Forestry, and so on. It sees the totality of the public interest becoming a force intended to ensure sustainable development in Canada and abroad.
Therefore, the commissioners have conceptually incorporated the environment in a global survival theme which brings together, perhaps for the first time, the ambitions and aspirations of developed countries with those of developing countries. No longer will the dichotomy exist; the two hemispheres are brought together with the theme of sustainable development. That I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, is the genius of this report. For the first time this dichotomy of interests, north and south, has been put aside and the theme of sustainable development has provided the common denominator for the totality of mankind.
According to the commissioners, change must occur along three basic tracks; placing on our national Governments the onus of implementing at home and abroad the report's recommendations; confirming the present mandate of the United Nations Environment Program and giving it new technical responsibilities; and three, by calling on the U.N. Secretary General to act globally through existing United Nations agencies in their totality. In other words, not by reinventing another bureaucracy or mechanism but by using better, and reorganizing, existing United Nations agencies which, as we know, are many and important but have not yet adopted, in their own way of thinking, budgeting and setting their own goals, the importance of sustainable development. This is a first in the history of the United Nations.
As with many other things in life, a task like this requires political will. I am sure that if national Governments, and Canada in particular, will generate pressure in the United Nations, governments will manage to bring the change about. There is only until October in time, of course, for governments to prepare themselves at the General Assembly, but it can be done.

May 15, 1987
Supply
The report outlines how to proceed from now in anticipation of this doubling of our planet's population. In order to get from here to there, one of the essential prerequisites is to rekindle the flame of international co-operation, which has a special meaning to Canada if one considers the difficulties we are having with acid rain and with other trans-boundary pollution problems experienced in the last decade or so. We do not want this report to become just another report. We do not want it to collect dust. The commission calls for a high level centre of leadership at the U.N. which can only be brought about by the political will generated among the nations which are members of the United Nations.
While national Governments are asked to reinforce the system, they ask why is it the responsibility and authority of the United Nations Secretary General? The commission at the same time is calling upon the Secretary General to constitute under his chairmanship a special United Nations board for sustainable development. In that sense, they give a signal that if the United Nations Secretary General were to assume this responsibility and develop it, then he would become the pivotal force, so to speak, for environment and development in his office at the head of the United Nations. His office would become the centre of three global preoccupations; one being peace, as well all know, the second being the environment, and the third being development. These are the three themes which would be the cement and the bond because of the community of interest in all member nations of the UN. Not one member nation of the UN would disagree with the fact that the main preoccupations globally today are these three points; peace, development and environment. In this sense, time is of the essence.
In her forward to this report, Madam Brundtland who, as you know, Mr. Speaker, is the Prime Minister of Norway, makes a number of interesting observations which I will quickly put forward for your consideration.
First, in the present times we have seen a deterioration in global co-operation which must be replaced by a return to multilateralism. That means co-operation between neighbouring nations in one region, globally as well. Second, the environment does not exist as a sphere separate from human actions, the environment is where we all live, and development is what we all do in attempting to improve our own lot within that abode called the environment. The two are inseparable. Third, many of the development paths of the industrialized nations are clearly unsustainable. I repeat, they are unsustainable, one of Madam Brundtland's points. The development decision of these countries, because of their great economic and political power, could have a profound effect upon the ability of all people to sustain human progress for generations to come.
What is needed is a new approach to economic growth, a new era so to speak; growth that is forceful and at the same time socially and environmentally sustainable. You can see the importance of the word "sustainable" which pops up almost on every page of this report, the theme of finding ways to
maintain sustainable growth that can accommodate larger and larger numbers of inhabitants on this planet.
The commissioners, as I mentioned to you, Mr. Speaker, came from widely differing backgrounds. After three years and starting with a variety of different approaches, they managed to produce a unanimous report. That is no minor feat considering the background, the education, the outlooks and the cultural values of the 22 commissioners from five different regions of the world.
In the report, the commissioners address governments, private enterprise, industry and labour. First and foremost are people, in particular, the young people of the world. Madam Brundtland stresses the fact that the world's teachers will have a crucial role to play in bringing this report to the attention of the young.
The report has an optimistic tone in contrast to other environmental documents. It expresses the belief that people can build a future more prosperous, more just and more secure. Rather than predicting ever increasing environmental decay, poverty and hardship, the commission seized the possibility for a new era of economic growth based on policies that sustain and expand the environmental resource base. Such growth is absolutely essential to relieve the great poverty in many parts of the world poverty which is deepening in much of the developing world.
The commissioners give the reader an urgent message based on the latest and best scientific evidence that the time has come to take the decisions needed to secure the resources to sustain this and coming generations. What is required is a spirit of international co-operation with the future of mankind in mind.
As you know, it is an historic fact that over time humanity has developed loyalties with greater and greater scope, Mr. Speaker. We started with the family, of course, and developed loyalties within the family. We then went to the clan to which we belong, then to the region, and eventually in the political history of mankind we developed the concept of nation and loyalty to the nation. In recent decades we have developed the new concept of loyalty to groups of nations and to the United Nations in general.
The authors of this report point to a new loyalty, a loyalty to the planet. The test of this report and of the political will in the parliaments of the world will be whether we will have the ability and foresight to make these loyalties ours, not only in theory but in practice. That will be the real test. The report refers to who the beneficiaries of the report will be.
I notice that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I wonder whether, with the consent of the House, I could be permitted to carry on.

speechtext:
As the Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) is suggesting, their children and grandchildren would benefit as well.
In the implementation of the ideas of this report, which may take several generations of parliamentarians, in the time period leading up to the launching of the commission, during the life of the commission, and from then on, there are very good reasons for Canada to develop the same relationship with the World Commission on the Environment and Development as Switzerland has developed with the Red Cross over the last century.
We certainly have a stake in that which is in this report because our well-being depends so much on natural resources. If we can turn things around in a manner which will enable us to better develop our relationship with our natural resources, our economy will benefit as well as our well-being.
The process will not be as simple as I have outlined it so far. The process will require changes in thinking, in behaviour and in structures. If the changes in thought take place, structures can change, particularly governmental structures with regard to how we govern and organize ourselves. As Madam Brundt-land emphasized very strongly in her report, there would be a return to multilateralism and an international spirit of cooperation.
I will move on to Chapter 12, the action chapter of the report, in which six priorities are outlined. The first priority deals with getting at the sources, in other words, to begin to focus on the source of the problem of how we affect the resources rather than on the effects, as we often do.
The second priority is to deal with the effects. The importance of that can, of course, be the subject of another intervention.
The third priority is the importance of assessing the global risks. In this respect Canada is playing a leadership role right now under the auspices of the present Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) on the question of the depletion of the ozone. We congratulate the Minister on that very fine initiative because the depletion of the ozone is one of the global risks which we must face. In addition to that we must be concerned about the warming up of temperatures, better known as the greenhouse effect.
Supply
The fourth priority is the importance of making informed choices. There is a phenomenal range of informed choices which must be made through the actions of NGOs, teachers and governments in informing the public and so on.
The fifth priority is to provide legal means. This again is the subject of a speech by itself which the Hon. Member for York South-Weston will tackle later this afternoon. The sixth priority is investing in our future. There are a number of very important considerations with regard to this which time does not permit me to put on the record.
I would like to put the following paragraph from page 336 of the report forward for your consideration because I think it is so important. It reads:
Nations, industrial and developing, that did not make these investments have paid much more in terms of damage costs to human health, property, natural resources and the environment.
And these costs continue to rise at an accelerating pace. Indeed, countries that have not yet instituted strong programmes now face the need for very large investments. Not only do they need to roll back the first generation of environmental damage-
This is something which we are doing on the Niagara River and the St. Clair River and are trying to do with acid rain.
-they also need to begin to catch up with the rising incidence of future damage. If they do not, their fundamental capital assets, their environmental resources, will continue to decline.
What are these environmental resources? Obviously they are water, soil, forests, and all the other natural resources on which humanity depends that are so essential in maintaining the growth and well-being of the human species.
What should the response be to this report? The Government could and should direct each Deputy Minister to review the content of Our Common Future and report to their respective Ministers which recommendations in this report their Department can adopt and incorporate by way of a change of internal policy, and which they cannot adopt, and to indicate the reasons why.
Further, the Government can, as it has already, form a task force on the environment and the economy which has the mandate to consider this report; the group presently consists of seven Ministers of the Environment, provincial and federal, representatives from industry, from NGOs and one academic. We deplore very much the absence of labour from that committee. The committee could be expanded to include other people as well, but time does not permit me to go into that.
The Government could also ensure that the basic recommendations which impinge upon Canada's performance in our common future become standing items on the agenda of the meetings of the committee of provincial and federal environment and resource Ministers from across the country. That is a must.
Further, sustainable development should be made a permanent item on the agenda of the regular meetings of the First Ministers when they meet at regular intervals. Parliament could launch a joint committee of the House and Senate to ensure that the basic concepts of this report are known to

May 15, 1987
Supply
the public, and to solicit and invite suggestions and input from Canadians at large. That in itself would be a very interesting and exciting parliamentary experience.
Looking beyond our boundaries, the report makes a recommendation which I commend to you very highly, and that is that Canada should develop an environmental foreign policy. As we develop a peace policy we should certainly start to think in terms of an environmental foreign policy.
What can be done outside government does not require much elucidation. I would only say that non-governmental organizations could perform a major role, as well as interested individuals and groups and native groups who will become increasingly interested in finding ways of supporting the transition that lies ahead to an economy based on sustainable development.
As well, a suggestion could be made to establish a "futures committee", comprised of leaders in business and labour, in environmental organizations, in the educational sector, in the arts and communications to look at the concepts of sustainable development as they apply to Canada and the globe, and to tap new ideas and resources. Public education will be the key in the adoption and implementation of what is in this report.
It is absolutely essential to provide a kit for teachers that will give them an understanding of Our Common Future so they will be able to pass the message on to the children and youth in our school systems across the nation.
The reason for this motion today is to provide for a constructive debate on the report of the World Commission on the Environment and Development only 19 days after it was released in London. We do this in order to bring to the attention of the House and Canadians at large the concepts involved in this very crucial and important document, and to register and reinforce the urgency of the situation and the overwhelming need to act now if we are to assure the survival of the human race in the long term.
In October of this year the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) will be addressing the General Assembly of the United Nations to deliver Canada's response to this report. Many of our colleagues who have attended international conferences will know that Canada is looked upon for leadership in global environmental, peace and security matters. To this end, we on this side of the House urge the Minister of the Environment, with the help of his Cabinet colleagues and Members of Parliament, provincial Governments, public groups and NGOs, to develop not just a message of process and policy but of specific projects and concrete examples on how to reach the goals of sustainable development within the systems of three levels of Government in our nation, as basically advanced by the Brundtland Report.
I will conclude by quoting the last paragraph of that report which states:
We are unanimous in our conviction that the security, well being, and very
survival of the planet depend on such changes, now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S O. 82- THE ENVIRONMENT- REQUEST THAT THE GOVERNMENT ENDORSE, ADOPT AND ADVOCATE, AT HOME AND ABROAD, THE GOALS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE BRUNDTLAND REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me as Parliamentary Secretary, to speak today on behalf of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) on this very important subject. We are discussing today the work of the World Commission on the Environment and Development, commonly known as the Brundtland report. That report is named, of course after the Prime Minister of Norway. 1 had the very great pleasure of welcoming some musicians from Norway just a few days before the report was tabled in London. I must say the Norwegian people are very proud of the report being named after their Prime Minister.
We are all in agreement with the World Commission Report on the Environment and Development. It is a major step towards tackling global environmental challenges. There are a number of serious challenges which affect us all, such as acid rain, air and water quality, pollution, toxic wastes, to name a few. However, the commission focuses on the most important challenge of all, and that is the challenge of encouraging economic growth while protecting our ecological environment.
Economic growth together with environmental protection is the theme of this report called Our Common Future. Today we have an opportunity to consider the environment on a global plane. By providing people in Canada and around the world with this report the commission has performed a most useful function. The presence of Dr. Maurice Strong and Jim MacNeill, Secretary General, both Canadians, ensured that the commission was made well aware of Canadian concerns.
May 15, 1987

In choosing Canada as one of only four countries in which to hold public hearings, the commission chose wisely. Canada is a unique resource for any environment related studies. There are several reasons for this. First, this is a very large country. It is the world's second largest land mass embracing, as it does, three oceans, the Atlantic Ocean, the Pacific Ocean and the Arctic Ocean. Since we are managers of such a large part of the globe's real estate, how we manage what we have has to be important to the rest of the world.
Much of Canada rests on the Precambrian Shield which sustains vast forests and pockets of mineral wealth, but we have a relatively small population. In the West, farmers are plagued by drought, falling water-tables and unstable soils. The mountains in the west, magnificent in their majesty, restrict two-thirds of the population of that area to the lower Fraser River valley. The north is dominated by cold, dry tundra. In fact, the north, because of the limitations of its ecosystems, has a very delicate environmental balance. Economic development must therefore be undertaken with care.
Let us look more closely at the reality behind the popular image of Canada as a country of hewers of wood and drawers of water, at the parts of the country-the Province of Ontario in which we are sitting today, the Province of Quebec which we can see across the river, the eastern provinces, including Prince Edward Island, where once there was a sea of white pine, wave after wave of trees that grew so tall that they seemed the very pillars holding up our skies. It was not uncommon to fell trees that were 15 metres high and perhaps three metres in diameter. We need to do more to replant what has been harvested. As a result lumbermen have been reduced to cutting black spruce 1,500 kilometres northeast of Ottawa in our less fertile forests.
Within our mammoth land is a diversity that parallels much of the rest of the world; geographically, climatically, economically and culturally. There are within Canada greater differences than exist between entire countries elsewhere in the world. Looking at Canada is like viewing conditions around the globe, as if we offered the commission a world visit for the cost of a single airfare; from virgin forests in South Moresby to the fragile high Arctic to the towering but delicate sand dunes of the Cavendish Beaches; from Quebec City, a UNESCO heritage site, to the Old Port of Montreal; and from Toronto, which is now praised as North America's most livable large city, to the Scarborough Bluffs which are on the edge of Lake Ontario just south of my riding, right to Vancouver.
Beyond what Canada is lies what Canada does. What Canada does best goes to the very heart of this debate. We were pioneers and have now become seasoned experts in the reality of environmental interdependence. Whether acid or toxic rain, nuclear radiation, or in any other form, pollution moves around our planet irrespective of the maps we have made and the national flags in which we wrap our pride.
Supply
Pollution moves upward and outward as well, piercing the layers of the stratosphere nature gave us as a protective blanket and threatening the purity of space beyond our space.
Nowhere is this more obvious than in the shared Canadian-American environment where, on a less global scale, two countries are linked by waterways, mountain ranges and even by wind patterns. We in Canada have, with our American friends, pioneered international co-operation. We have resorted to every form of co-operative measure to keep each other's garbage off our own front lawns. We have reciprocal laws, bilateral mechanisms, agreements, treaties and regular summits between heads of state.
We are very pleased with the recent Niagara River memorandum of understanding signed by four levels of Government: Ontario, New York, United States and Canada. There is a Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement and, of course, the International Joint Commission which has been dealing with transboundary water boundaries and now soil, pollution, air, and, of course, the high water levels that are of particular importance today.
I recognize, of course, that these Canadian-U.S. initiatives are the result of interaction between two wealthy countries. By contrast, the commission faced environmental questions in countries where poverty is an economic reality. Countries are forced to sacrifice their precious natural resources for urgent short-term purposes at the expense of their immediate environment and future generations.
The consequences of encroaching on our environmental capital have been identified by the report of the commission. Some of them include the greenhouse effect, which threatens to overheat the world by wrapping it in a layer of carbon dioxide; the dangers of a nuclear winter imposed on us by war or by accident; arctic haze, which reminds us that airborne pollution travels thousands of miles, and even countries away from its industrial origins; lessened genetic diversity, which may eliminate potential sources of medications that alleviate human suffering; and the destruction of the natural heritage so essential to human survival. Humankind's life support systems-the air we breathe, the water we drink, the soil that provides our food-is under seige. A steadily growing population means that more and more people will be trying to live on less and less environmental capital, much of which is under environmental strain.
The commission report asks what can be done to stop this spiral. Despite the best intentions, foreign aid and favourable trade arrangements, the industrialized world has work to do in assisting developing countries and nations to solve their root problems. We live in a fortunate country blessed with a wealth of resources and opportunities. That wealth gives us a unique role to play in helping less developed countries reach their potential.
Part of that role includes providing development assistance that takes into account both economic development and environmental protection. Canada's development agency,

May 15, 1987
Supply
CIDA, now budgets 20 per cent to 25 per cent of all funds for bilateral aid projects to the environmental concerns associated with them. That is a significant part of the CIDA budget. In addition, all Canadian aid projects in the Third World are subject to an in-depth environmental assessment. The Government is also tackling our own domestic environmental issues.
One of Canada's most troubling environmental problems is that of toxic wastes. The Department of the Environment is now preparing legislation to help manage toxic chemicals through their entire life cycle, from formulation, manufacture, distribution, sale and use, to eventual disposal.
Even as that legislation is now being developed, there is growing concern, because of toxic rain, about the presence of lethal chemicals in the environment. If we are to take action, and we are, we will find solid ground on which to tackle this problem in concrete terms. The commission has already identified anticipation and prevention of economic environmental mismanagement as essential, and I certainly agree.
The Minister of the Environment established the National Task Force on the Environment and the Economy to improve the co-ordination of economic and environmental decisionmaking. Further, the Minister of the Environment is also ensuring that his cabinet colleagues take environmental considerations into account when federal economic decisions are made.
In Canada, studies show that in all of the policy questions that have dominated the public agenda since the end of World War II, attitudes have shifted on only one major issue, the environment. And even in respect of the environment there is a need to increase an understanding of the true state of the environment and of the importance of preventive measures.
We have to ensure that today's consumers of the environment, and tomorrow's, understand the consequences of the chemical society, of the overfished lake, of the carelessly set forest fire; and moreover, we have to make the consumer aware not just of the problem but of how we as individuals can help prevent it.
A better understanding by youth is especially important, for half of the present and all of the future belongs to our youth.
The State of the Environment report, released by the Department of the Environment in May of 1986 is an analysis of the Canadian environment, over time and on the total system, on a stress-response basis, not on the basis of individual problems in specific parts of the country. While there have been such surveys in other countries, the State of the Environment report in Canada remains the first of its kind anywhere in the world, both for its thoroughness and for its holistic approach.
With the release of this report. Our Common Future, we have a global State of the Environment report.
Canadians, for their part, participated in the events leading to the report during the visit of the commission to Canada last summer. We see throughout the report the importance placed on the Canadian input. Throughout the pages of the report, many Canadians are quoted, including the federal Minister of the Environment. I should like to quote some of the words of the Minister of the Environment, as set out in the report, as follows:
The world's environmental problems are greater than the sum of those in each
country. Certainly, they can no longer be dealt with purely on a nation-state
basis.
The commission met with Canadians in Vancouver, Edmonton, Toronto, Quebec City, and Halifax. It also visited Fort McMurray, South Moresby, and James Bay, all very important parts of Canada from an environmental standpoint. In addition, the commission held two days of public hearings in Ottawa, for the purpose of hearing submissions from Canadians from across the country.
During the public hearings in Ottawa the commission received 124 written submissions. At the same time, there were discussions with 140 individuals, representing industry, labour, native and environmental groups, the voluntary sector, and the general public.
This Government welcomes the clear demonstration of interest and concern expressed by Canadians. We are going to be sure that the voice of Canada, and of Canadians, is heard in the follow-up to this report.

The Canadian Arctic and the ice mass associated with

the whole north polar region play a dramatic role in terms of the earth's climate. It is reflected in many ways relative to rainfall, aridity, soil erosion, and a whole host of other things.
