speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate in this very important debate. At the outset, let me say that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) was unable to be here today. He very much wanted to participate in the debate, but a long-standing invitation to a speaking engagement in his riding prevented him from being
here. He very much regrets it. However, I do not regret it, because it gives me the opportunity to speak on the motion.
I also wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for introducing the motion and for encouraging the creation of the World Commission on Environment and Development and its report entitled Our Common Future. He has played a positive role in that regard, allowing for a very positive and important report to be issued by the international commission.
The commission warns us of the environmental disasters that are waiting to happen. It outlines for the public of the world some of the social, economic and environmental trends. In doing so, I think it functions in a very important way. It gives us a warning that we should heed. For example it says:
In terms of absolute numbers there are more hungry people in the world than ever before, and their numbers are increasing. So are the numbers of those who cannot read or write, the numbers of those without safe water or safe and sound homes, and the numbers who are short of woodfuel with which to cook and warm themselves. The gap between the rich and the poor nations is widening-not shrinking-and there is little prospect, given present trends and institutional arrangements, that this process will be reversed.
It goes on to outline that:
Each year another 6 million hectares of productive dryland turns into worthless desert. More than 1 1 million hectares of forests are destroyed yearly, and this, over 3 decades, would equal an area the size of India.
It talks about acid rain.
The burning of fossil fuels puts into the atmosphere carbon dioxide which is causing gradual global warming.
This is the greenhouse effect. It maintains that in the early part of the next century the greenhouse effect will increase average global temperatures enough to shift agricultural production areas, raise sea levels to flood coastal cities, disrupt national economies and so forth. It also warns of the depletion of the ozone layer and the effect this will have on increasing human and animal cancers.
The commission did not deal with that area I would call social and psychological pollution. We are living in an age of tremendous social and economic change. You start out in life after some training, never being certain that the job you have trained for will be there. Most people realize now that they will have to change jobs two or three times in a lifetime. We have also seen that the social glue holding communities, societies and families together is now also disappearing. Individual human beings are somewhat in a free flow. A tremendous state of instability exists among our social institutions. There are increases in crime rates, depressions, mental breakdowns and suicides, particularly, and alarmingly, among the young. We have psychopaths who wander the streets and commit mindless murders. These are all symptoms of a society becoming unglued. They are examples of social and psychological pollution.
There is no doubt that we are living in an age of tremendous change, unparalleled in the history of the human race. I
May 15, 1987

remember a few years ago attending a conference in Vancouver listening to the eminent American futurologist, Buckminster Fuller. He was explaining to us that all of the important discoveries made in the history of the human race had been made in his lifetime-in his lifetime, Mr. Speaker.
So fast are the rates of change that nobody is unaffected. The industrialized developed world is also finding the effects of those rapid economic, social and cultural changes. It is obvious that present social institutions in many respects are not capable of dealing with these rapid changes. There are social institutions based on a mind-set in vogue as we entered this century, yet the events that have occurred in this century have made many of those mind-sets obsolete and dangerous.
The commission talks about-and I was very pleased to read this-viable, sustainable social and economic institutions. It talks about sustainable development and growth. In that word "sustainable" lies a whole world of different thoughts, a whole different civilization, a whole different way of doing things, living lives and doing economic and social activities that put a roof over our heads and bread on the table. In that word lies the real importance of this document. In many ways we live in two different worlds. We are all caught in it, particularly we as Members of Parliament.
Let me give two examples. The commission talks about energy, and the need to plan. Oil is a finite resource for which alternate energies must be developed. Conservation has to be dealt with. Last night when I was preparing for my remarks I came across an old copy of the December 1983 report put out by Canertech, a division of Petro-Canada, dealing with alternate energies. In its report it states that alternate energy and energy conservation will create more jobs, save so many billions of dollars to the consumer and so forth. In a recommendation it says that the days of burning fossil fuels have to be numbered. A greenhouse effect is forming that will totally change the climatic patterns and therefore the social and economic patterns of this globe. We cannot continue to put out garbage. Other ways have to be found to dispose of it.
The warnings are there. Yet we live in this other world. We live in this world of jobs in which the economy of your Province of Alberta, Mr. Speaker, and my Province of Saskatchewan are almost in ruins because of the oil price collapse. We stand here in the House of Commons asking for more assistance for the industry, yet we know that that industry over the long term is not sustainable. It is not a life forming sustainable industry because it is threatening the very atmosphere of this globe.
The other example, is the field of agriculture. The commission points out rightly that the heavy subsidization of agriculture in the developed world has meant more planting from fence line to fence line, putting land into production that should never be in production, with the use of chemicals and fertilizer-mining the soil, so to speak. We in western Canada know this. Commissions and studies have warned us that one cannot continue doing this forever and ever. We have a finite world. Our resources are finite. The soil is finite. We do not
Supply
have an infinite world in which we can continue to exploit the soil as people have in the past. On the other hand, when wheat prices fall, my colleagues and I ask for further assistance from the Government. I raise this in all honesty because if we take a look we will recognize the contradictions that exist. We are living in two different worlds simultaneously. They are worlds in conflict and worlds apart.
The commission talks about a new type of world that we have to move into if we are to survive as a human species. We are still in this other world which assumes that our resources are infinite. We are in a world which demands short-term decision making, not long-term, meaning governments from poll to poll and election to election. We should be guided and motivated by that. With business it is the bottom line at the end of the month or at the end of the year. That is what shareholders are concerned about.
If we as a human species are to survive we have to expand our consciousness. We must begin to realize that what we do in one place has an effect on other places around the globe. We have to expand our collective consciousness to realize that what we do today will affect tomorrow and the days after. We have to expand our consciousness so that we begin to realize that things have effects and then act accordingly in the best interests of future generations. The institutions, of which we are a part, force us to act on a short-term basis and not in the best interests of the global village, and not necessarily in the best interests of tomorrow and the heritage of our children.
I do not know what the solutions to these problems are. If, for example, the oil industry is not a sustainable industry in the long term, we must be able to offer a social net so that those employed in that industry can find other meaningful employment. We must, for example, allow for the evolution of another form of agriculture that is on a smaller scale, is sustainable and would allow people to live economically viable lives in a rural setting without being forced into the cities. However, evolving those programs and policies requires a different mind-set, a different consciousness, a different civilization. I hope that this report is a step in that direction and I hope that this debate in the House is a step in that direction.
The human race has embarked on a journey into the unknown. The old patterns no longer fit. It is not a question of the old ideologies, public versus private ownership, because either can be as unconscious of the environment and its workers. It is not a matter of workers versus capital because they are both motivated by their own self interests. Workers want and need their jobs and incomes, and capital, of course, requires a rate of return. It is not a question of left versus right. New thinking is required.
This new thinking must be co-operative. People must work together in the common interest and for the common good. That surely is the first priority. If we are to evolve sustainable economic, social and political institutions, those institutions

May 15, 1987
Supply
must surely be built on a co-operative model and not on an adversarial one. That is true of labour and capital and of our justice and political systems.
It is the adversarial nature of our present civilization that in many ways creates the bottle-necks. Humanity must evolve more stable and life-sustaining forms of social institutions.
I am particularly happy that the commission addressed international arms expenditures. The commission states that out of a world economy of some $16 trillion, about $1 trillion gets funnelled into the development of arms, the machinery of death. Over all this hangs the danger of a nuclear war and the destruction of the human race as we know it. Surely of all the environmental dangers that face humanity, that is the most important one. The resolution of that danger again requires a different mind-set. It is not East versus West, the communists against the capitalists, the Russians against the Americans. It is a question of our mutual survival. It is a question of addressing the fears of nation states and political and cultural alliances, not through the production of more deadly means of destruction but through the development of sustaining forms of social, economic and political institutions.
The commission pointed out how ironic it is that because of decisions that were made, the deserts in the Sahara are increasing at such an alarming rate that more destruction is being done there than would have been done if an army had invaded and practised the worst kind of scorched-earth policy. Against such an army, we would invest hundreds of millions if not billions of dollars. Yet hardly a gesture has been made to block the desert. How strange our priorities for surviving in this day and age.
In creating those institutions which are meaningful in what I would call a post-industrial society, we must see that they are co-operative in nature. They must take a long-term view of decisions that are made. They must imply planning and care and the proper husbandry, not only of our soil but of our resources and our environment. This requires an intelligence in the decision-making process. It will be a long journey and the human race has embarked on that journey. There is no turning back. As we come to the end of the century, we will continue to meet increasing crises in food and starvation, environmental damage on a global or a regional scale and further economic, social and psychological upheavals. These are indeed very dangerous times.
The members of the commission and 1 have come to the same conclusion, that there is hope that the human race has the capability of developing those institutions that are sustainable. The human race can develop a higher level of consciousness and all men and women on the face of this planet can begin to benefit from the richness of human intelligence, the vastness of our resources and the beauty of our mother, this planet Earth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his very valid question. I am not certain what the answer is to all of this. Of course if Third World countries are able to export more and earn more income they can increase their standards of living and have the resources to deal with the environmental problems which will arise as they develop.
Another voice inside of me says that that was the same argument used to get them into forms and patterns of development which now have them so badly in debt that there is more hunger now than there ever was before in those countries. They were lured into this pattern of development and got into cash crops. They now have surpluses of coffee and sugar but not enough basic substances to feed their people on a day-today basis. There is starvation in the midst of plenty.
Something has gone wrong with the pattern of development. We must make certain that whatever pattern of development we suggest to Third World countries will not put them deeper in the pit than they are now. So far we have not been very helpful to them.
We hear everyone saying that we need more international trade in order to balance our payments and create jobs and prosperity at home. That is what the Americans are saying and that is what they are saying in Brazil and all over Europe. If everyone is going to be exporting more, who is going to be importing? There is a myth that the more we export the more wealthy we will become. Who is going to import? I have not heard of one country saying that it will import more.
Something else is amiss, Mr. Speaker. I do not have all the answers but before we find answers we will have to explode some of the myths. There are a few around which deserve to be discredited and questioned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it somewhat strange that Conservative Members of Parliament would deny unanimous consent to allow questions to be asked of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) after several members of the Conservative Party complained that they did not have the opportunity to ask questions, and particularly after the Hon. Member for Davenport indicated a willingness to answer any questions which might be presented to him.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this debate this afternoon. I am very proud and pleased that the Parliament of Canada is debating the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development entitled Our Common Future less than three weeks after it was tabled and made public in London. The credit, of course, must go to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport, the critic for the Ministry of the Environment for the Official Opposition, for taking the initiative to bring this matter before Parliament to allow all parliamentarians the opportunity to discuss this document which will be discussed world-wide for the remainder of this century.
The report, Our Common Future, is probably one of the most important documents ever produced because it addresses the very future of the world. The Hon. Member for Davenport has moved what I consider to be an extremely important motion which, with your permission, I would like to read. The motion reads:
That this House urge the Government to endorse, adopt and advocate, at home and abroad, the goals and recommendations of the Report of the World Commission on Environment and Development (Brundtland Report), entitled "Our Common Future";
That this Report, dealing with global concerns, challenges and endeavours, be adopted as the central policy of the federal Government, its agencies and commissions; and
That the Minister of the Environment advocate the spirit and the substance of this Report at the coming General Assembly of the United Nations on behalf of Canadians and of the global community, thus continuing Canada's tradition of giving leadership on environmental matters.
If this motion were to be put to a vote, 1 suspect that it would receive unanimous consent of the House.

May 15, 1987
Supply
I believe the report Our Common Future is probably one of the most important documents that will be discussed in Parliaments throughout the world, including the countries in the western world and behind the Iron Curtain.
When the report speaks of our common future, its authors are not speaking specifically with regard to the future of any particular country but are speaking of the future of humanity and the world as we know it.
The point has been made that the world is finite, that we can grow only so much before we run out of room and deplete the necessary resources to sustain growth.
By the year 2025, the population of the world will double. Presently, the population of the world is 4.5 billion. In a short 38 years, the population will be nine billion, and that fact alone would suggest very strongly that every Parliament, every parliamentarian, every politician and every person in the world must address the question of the future of the globe. It is not only timely that we in Canada should be discussing this report, it is timely for the world.
In 1983, the United Nations General Assembly took a timely decision and established the World Commission on Environment and Development, to study and recommend action on global trends which require urgent attention. Let us examine these trends. One trend is the doubling of the population in 38 years. The report made several other important observations. For example, there are more hungry people in the world today than ever before and more will be hungry with each passing day.
Canada is not immune to the problem of hunger. Members will know that there are food banks in Canada and some of our fellow Canadians suffer the indignity of standing in line for food. There is a problem with poverty and hunger here in Canada, and when we speak of these problems that exist in the world, we must recognize that while we, as Canadians, are fortunate, we are not immune from each of these problems.
The commission also recognized that the gap between the rich and the poor nations is widening rather than narrowing. Each year, another six million hectares of productive dry land turn into worthless desert. More than 11 million hectares of forest are destroyed yearly.
Acid rain kills forests and lakes, damages buildings, structures, monuments, and acidifies water and soil. We in Canada are blessed by the environment. We are indeed fortunate to have some of the most beautiful country anywhere in the world.
However, our environment is threatened. Our lakes and forests are being threatened because of the problem of acid rain. We in the Opposition, through our critic on the environment, have been working very hard to ensure that this issue is treated as a top priority.
The commission also observed the problem with the greenhouse effect, which is the burning of fossil fuels which
puts carbon dioxide into the atmosphere causing gradual global warming. By early next century this phenomenon may increase average temperatures enough to shift agricultural production areas, raise sea levels to flood coastal cities, and disrupt national economies.
The commission also observed that industrial and agricultural activities release toxic substances into the human food chain and into underground water tables where removal is virtually impossible.
The commissioners found that the separation of economic development issues from environmental issues is a shortsighted policy. Many forms of development erode the environmental resource upon which they must be based. Environmental degradation can undermine economic development.
Poverty is a major cause and effect of global environmental problems. Attempts to deal with environmental problems without a broader perspective, encompassing the factors underlying world poverty and international inequality are becoming futile.
These main concerns led to the establishment of the commission some three or four years ago. Linked to, but outside the control of, governments and the UN system, the commission which was headed by Harlem Brundtland, pursued three objectives. They were: first, to re-examine the critical environment and development issues and to formulate realistic proposals for dealing with them; second, to propose new forums of international co-operation on these issues that will influence policies and events; and third, to raise the levels of understanding and commitment to action of individuals, volunteer organizations, businesses, institutes, and Governments.
The World Commission on Environment and Development consisted of 22 individuals drawn from five continents. I am pleased to say that the commission consisted of two very eminent Canadians, Mr. Maurice Strong and Mr. Jim MacNeill, who contributed tremendously to the report Our Common Future.
The commission held public hearings throughout the world. Observing that many development trends leave increasing numbers of people poor while at the same time degrading the environment, the commissioners pursued the question: "How can such development serve next century's world of twice as many people relying on the same environment?" As the hearings and meetings progressed, the commissioners came to view development not just in the restricted context of economic growth in developing countries. They concluded that a new development path was required, one which sustained human progress not just in a few places for a few years, but for the entire planet into the distant future. Thus the term "sustainable development" is a goal not just for the developing nations, but for industrialized nations as well.
The conclusions of this report are somewhat of a departure from previous thought in the area. Not long ago there was a general opinion that co-operation between the environment
May 15, 1987

and economic development was not possible. Many people cited gloomy statistics and were not at all optimistic about the future.
This report says that the environment can sustain economic growth and that the goals must be to ensure that economic growth occurs while considering the impact on the environment. In the Chairman's foreword to the report entitled Our Common Future, Mrs. Brundtland makes a number of interesting observations. She says in part, and I quote:
After a decade and a half of a standstill or even deterioration in global cooperation, I believe the time has come for higher expectations, for common goals pursued together, for an increased political will to address our common future.
We are here for a short period of time in the scheme of things. The average life span today in this country is age 65 years to 70 years. When we speak of the environment, we are talking about the future, not only the future of our children, our grandchildren and the generations to follow but the future of the world. All too often we become preoccupied with things which affect our country and our well-being simply in the short run.
Of course it is important to talk about the unemployment rate and the inflation rate. However, all too often issues dealing with the environment are put on the back burner. What this report, and hopefully this debate, will do is to put the issue of the environment in the forefront to ensure that not only this Parliament but people throughout the world think about the future of the world so that as we continue to grow, as our population increases, and the population of the world doubles in the next 38 years, this planet will be able to survive. In effect, what we are talking about is the survival of the planet.
The two world powers, the United States and the Soviet Union, are spending billions and billions of dollars in the arms race. Other nations in the world are spending billions of dollars as well to build arms to defend themselves. But who is spending money and resources to protect themselves not from one another but from the ultimate destruction of the world? The ultimate destruction will not come by war but because our environment might become destroyed making it impossible for human life to continue. Would it not be a Utopia if all those resources used today for building nuclear weapons and arms, defence systems and star wars systems could be spent on the environment? Would it not be great if we could deal with the problems of acid rain which are articulated in the report?
As the report points out, there is a way of ensuring the continued existence of humanity in this world. All that is necessary is the political will. The World Commission on Environment and Development quite correctly points out that the political will is not there at present. There must be political will in order to pursue some of the recommendations and objectives of this particular report. I suppose one of the reasons the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) presented his
Supply
motion to the House is to try not only to raise the consciousness of this Parliament and the country on this particular issue but also to try to urge every parliamentarian to somehow acquire the political will in order to ensure that we can continue to grow while at the same time protecting and improving our environment.
The environment should not be a partisan issue. Unfortunately, at times it does become a partisan issue, but such is the nature of our adversarial system and our Parliament. However, I am sure all three political Parties can work together in pursuing some of the very important objectives which are outlined in this report.
The remarkable achievement of the report is that it lucidly advances the debate on the environment from a protection to a survival theme. People have to become aware that we are talking about survival. We are not simply talking about protecting our lakes, our forests and our soil. We are talking about the future of humanity. In effect, we are talking about the survival of the world. How do we ensure sustainable development on this planet while the global population will double between now and the year 2025? Some of us, God willing, may still be alive in the year 2025. Our children and grandchildren will be alive. Future generations will be born in the years which follow the year 2025. Looking at this prospect, the commissioners place the environment not in the context of just one public interest competing with others and at times even in conflict with the economy. The commissioners lead the reader to conclude that the only sensible answer to global problems is through the careful management of the natural resources available on earth and man's impact on them in a manner which ensures nature's generative capacity.
The environment is thus brought to the very centre of economic activity and becomes a pre-condition for development. The dichotomy which has plagued some policy makers so far, that there is a choice to be made between the economy and the environment, is put neatly to rest, hopefully once and for all.
In this scenario, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) becomes an agent for sustainable development, as do other political forces such as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), and so on.
In closing, let me say that it is not sufficient simply to have a Minister of the Environment and a Ministry of the Environment, and to say that this particular Ministry and this particular Minister are responsible for the environment and that somehow other Ministers of the Crown should not address that issue. What this report is saying is that each and every Minister of the Crown and, indeed, every policy maker in Canada, when deciding public policy, must ask: "What impact will my decision have on the environment? How can I ensure that we can sustain growth?" I simply ask Hon. Members opposite to support this very worthwhile motion which was presented by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport. I

May 15, 1987

am grateful to have had the opportunity to participate in this important debate.

The previous speaker mentioned a few points, one of which was that this debate is non-partisan and probably should remain that way. It is a concern which all Members of the House share. The importance of the environment to all Canadians, and to the whole world, is certainly supreme in our minds.
The Hon. Member mentioned the tremendous growth rate expected in the next 38 years. Our world population will increase from five billion to double that, and the report suggests that it may stabilize sometime in the next century in the eight billion to 14 billion person range. The report does note that 90 per cent of this growth will take place in the world's poorest nations, quite obviously putting very severe stress and pressure on the economies of already very fragile countries. Would the Hon. Member have specific recommendations as to how to approach this oncoming and very real problem?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously there is no quick and easy solution to the problem. I recognize that most of the growth will occur in the underdeveloped nations in terms of population. 1 suppose our immigration policy is a way in which we can assist to a large extent with regard to that particular problem. We have a population of some 25 million in Canada. We know, just in terms of land mass, that our country can accommodate millions and millions more individuals. Of course, our social programs may not.
The important conclusion from this report is that we can sustain growth, which is in opposition to a body of thought prevalent in the past which suggested that the world could not sustain the growth that will occur. Because of the fact that the population is about to double in 38 years there was a feeling of almost surrender, a feeling of despair that nothing could be done. What makes this report so important is that it concludes that we can sustain growth. It does not say that growth has to stop at some future point in time and that the environment will be adversely affected. This report says that we can continue to grow while at the same time protecting our environment.
If all the Governments of the world were to adopt some of the recommendations in the report, then we could have this sustainable growth and accommodate the population increase that is predicted over the next 20 or 30 years.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member mentions that our immigration policy could relieve this problem somewhat. In reality what we are looking at is an increase of five billion once the world population doubles. Our economy and our resources cannot offer very much assistance to that type of problem. I suggest that more effort will have to go into areas in which the expected growth will take place and that perhaps the focus should be on poorer countries and how we can assist
them in terms of their quality of growth. We also have to take into consideration the fragile nature of our world environment.
Does the Hon. Member care to offer specific suggestions for what we should be doing in the poorer countries of the world and how we can assist their quality of growth at a time when such assistance is very vital and much needed?

In my previous reply I was not suggesting that we can solve the problem simply by opening up our doors here in Canada. I was simply suggesting that there are ways that we can participate in this global strategy. There are quite a number of things that can be done.
What is important is that the report speaks of a new loyalty that is emerging. Whereas in the past we had loyalties to a particular region, to our country, for example, there is a new emerging loyalty which is articulated in the report. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S O. 82- THE ENVIRONMENT- REQUEST THAT THE GOVERNMENT ENDORSE, ADOPT AND ADVOCATE, AT HOME AND ABROAD, THE GOALS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE BRUNDTLAND REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on this major issue of the environment which is vital to Quebec and Canada, and of course, as you can appreciate, Mr. Speaker, to the riding of Trois-Rivieres and its residents.
As mentioned, last April 29 the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) received the report of the World Commission on the Environment and Development. It was a highlight in the history of the world ecological movement.
Last year Canada and the Conservative Government were delighted to play host to the World Commission on the Environment and Development, and we welcome their report entitled "Our Common Future". We will participate actively in the debate on the report which is on the agenda of the governing council of the United Nations environment program and that of the General Assembly of the United Nations.
Compared with other diagnoses made on the condition of the world, the World Commission on the Environment and Development report has a rather uncommon history. To begin with, the 21 commission members led by Mrs. Brundtland met with ordinary people, farmers, workers, students, tribesmen, shanty towm. residents as well as with heads of state, scientists, industry and financial leaders. Public hearings, free of official constraints, were also held in a number of cities, in 10 countries including, of course, Canada.
May 15, 1987

The Commission's mandate consisted of re-examining urgent problems for the environment and development; drafting proposals for innovative, concrete and realistic measures to try and resolve those problems; and also increasing public awareness of these problems.
Mr. Speaker, this mandate is unique in that it deals with the environment and development together instead of separately, as is customary at nearly all levels in international and governmental organizations.
Today, however, the connection between ecology and economy is becoming more and more apparent. The report is based on case histories, statistics, personal testimony by participants at the public hearings and scientific assessments, which give a clear picture of the close links that exist between matters as apparently diverse as debt payments and natural disasters, the arms race and the disappearance of tropical forests.
In additional to the Commission's public hearings and its meetings with political leaders and figures throughout the world, the Commission received 75 studies by experts on all aspects of environmental and development problems. It set up task forces with the best experts to be had, to draft recommendations on food security, industry, energy and law. These recommendations formed the basis for the report's 12 chapters, which cover new approaches to the environment and development, the concept of sustainable development, the role of the international economy, population and human resources, the common future of the world and the environment, and proposals for institutional and legal change.
Finally, a decision had to be made, and the Commission did in fact decide, to avoid pointing an accusing finger at certain Governments, leading some to predict that the report would be wishy-washy.
"Our goal was to create a debate on these questions at the highest level and to promote international co-operation on those questions that could rally the support of all parties", explained Jim MacNeill of Canada, the Secretary General of the Commission. "Putting governments on the defensive would do nothing to encourage co-operation. The major players would simply refuse to play."
"Wherever the Commission went in Canada, it heard people passionately express their concern at realizing that, in their own part of the world, something had gone wrong" continued Mr. MacNeill. "This gave the Commission members a particular motivation, a feeling of responsibility towards all these people."
This approach reflects the wishes of Mrs. Brundtland. A former Minister of the Environment in Norway and Leader of the Opposition when she was appointed to chair the Commission, Mrs. Brundtland became Prime Minister in May 1986. Two weeks later, she left for Canada with her Commission for eight days of public hearings.
Supply
The members are personally committed to this job, which they feel very strongly is of major importance, since the decisions to be made will determine mankind's future.
They do not see in this report the end of their assignment, but rather its beginning. They have been invited to submit their report next May to ministerial representatives of countries belonging to the European Community and the European Association for Free Trade.
Canada was one of the first countries to receive a copy of this report. Mr. Maurice Strong, a member of the Commission, presented the report to the Minister of the Environment on April 29, 1987, two days following its international release in London.
One of the purposes was to let the Governments peruse the report and be familiar with it when they take part next fall in the United Nations' debate. Another was to provoke public awareness and secure the support of the people for such important issues as the environment.
Canada shares the hopes of the World Commission on Environment and Development that the United Nations' debate will not mean the end of their efforts to build a more prosperous, fair and secure world. Canada supports the Commission's proposals to integrate the notion of sustainable development in current economic and assistance programs.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that, during the United Nations' debate scheduled for next fall, Canada intends to participate fully and actively in the discussions on these and other issues raised in the Brundtland report.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S O. 82- THE ENVIRONMENT- REQUEST THAT THE GOVERNMENT ENDORSE, ADOPT AND ADVOCATE, AT HOME AND ABROAD, THE GOALS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE BRUNDTLAND REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to start with some broad points which clearly emerge from the report entitled Our Common Future, a report of the World Commission on Environment and Development.
To be serious, it is, I think, a very difficult report for Members of Parliament to relate to. Its complexities are considerable. The extent of the subject matter which it looks at is quite widespread. However, there are some aspects of the report that I should like to highlight in my remarks.
The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), in his remarks, spoke of the optimistic tone through the report. And reading through the report itself, one can certainly see the optimism. We have such comments as the following: "We see instead the possibility for a new era of economic growth"-and this despite the problems of "environmental decay, poverty, and hardship in an ever more polluted world among ever decreasing resources".
The analysis goes on to say that the possibility for this new era has to be "based on policies that sustain and expand the environmental resource base". It goes on:
And we believe such growth to be absolutely essential to relieve the great
poverty that is deepening in much of the developing world.

May 15, 1987
Supply
But the Commission's hope for the future is conditional on decisive political action now to begin managing environmental resources to ensure both sustainable human progress and human survival.
We are not forecasting a future; we are serving a notice-an urgent notice based on the latest and best scientific evidence-that the time has come to take the decisions needed to secure the resources to sustain this and coming generations.
So, while it is a message of hope, it is very much, too, a message of urgency, a message which tells us, as societies, that we must start to review the policies that we now pursue, the structures of society that are now in place. We have to look at new directions and to put in place these new directions for the sake of future generations.
As someone who has worked in developing countries a great deal, 1 was particularly struck by those portions of the report dealing with the gross poverty which exists in many parts of the Third World. For instance, at one stage in the report, the commission speaks of the economic crisis which faces us all, a crisis which the commission says is based on the slow-down of economic expansion and the stagnation in world trade in the 1980s, something which has challenged the ability of all nations to react and adjust.
Here we have a diverse group of people from all parts of the world identifying, in powerful terms, problems in the world economy.
The developing countries have been particularly hard hit by this economic crunch. Between 1980 and 1984, according to the commission, developing countries lost about $55 billion in export earnings because of the fall in commodity prices.
As a consequence, there has been a period of slow growth in the world economy, a slow growth which has hit especially hard the poorer countries of the world, those countries which can least afford to experience economic stagnation.
Looking at the change in per capita Gross Domestic Product for the middle range developing countries, those countries that we are most concerned about, in many respects, and leaving the large countries aside, leaving the oil-producing countries aside, we see that since 1981, in every single solitary year up to 1985-and I suspect beyond, though we do not have the statistics before us to substantiate that-there has been an absolute decrease in the per capita Gross Domestic Product, a decrease which, in 1982, for instance, was as high as 3.1 per cent per capita.
In talking about our environmental concerns, Mr. Speaker, we have to do so against that backdrop of economic crisis. It is against that backdrop that we have to consider the economic solutions that will mesh with our environmental concerns.
As the report itself stresses, reforms at the international level are needed to enable us to deal simultaneously with economic and ecological aspects in ways that allow the world economy to stimulate the growth of the developing countries while giving greater weight to environmental concerns.
Such an agenda requires a deep commitment by all countries, from the satisfactory working of multilateral institutions
such as the development banks to the making and observance of international rules in fields such as trade and investment, and a constructive dialogue on the many areas where national issues do not immediately coincide.
It is possible for us as Members of Parliament to have a debate on a Friday afternoon like this about what is a very heartfelt, well organized and important document; but I think it is absolutely crucial that we bring back to earth here in Canada some of the concerns which are being discussed in this report.
It is not simply a matter of work and improvement at the international level. The report and the motion, which we would support if it were a votable motion, concern the need for us to do something about the serious and urgent environmental problems facing us in Canada without putting at risk the economic concerns of many of us.
In order to bring the debate down to earth, I will talk about three or four specific environmental concerns which I think Canadian Governments have not recognized as being serious or have not dealt with urgently, as the report suggests is badly required.
For instance, I should like to refer to the report of the International Joint Commission on the Great Lakes in Ontario because it is so easy for us to forget, after dramatic incidents like the St. Clair River crisis, that the basic problem goes on. In respect of the Great Lakes area, the report indicates that the intrusion of toxic chemicals on our lives, including the incidence of specific toxic chemical disasters, is occurring with greater impact and frequency. These occurrences cannot be viewed as systemic aberrations or something we can forget about. Rather, they may be the inevitable, if unintended, consequences of our industrialized societies. More toxic chemical-related incidents are therefore bound to occur. The questions thus become: how many, where, how serious will be the consequences, and what can be done to mitigate the production and use of toxic chemicals?
The report also suggests that we do not have a comprehensive solution in Canada in respect of the Great Lakes, one part of the body of freshwater lakes in the country. This represents a source of shame for us as a country. It is important to accept the urgency suggested in the Brundtland report. It asks us to do something not only about world problems but about the problems in our own backyard which so far we have not been able to tackle successfully. As far as I am concerned, that is certainly at the top of the list of crucial issues which need to be tackled and require the urgency essential to come up with some sort of solution or plan toward a solution, at the very least.
We must also talk about the extent of air pollution which exists in many communities across Canada. We have a predilection for looking at the United States and saying that
May 15, 1987

that country and its acid rain delays are the crucial environmental issues facing us. I frankly say that in community after community across the country, as is the case in my constituency and I suspect in the constituencies of many Hon. Members sitting in the House today, there are air pollution problems which are damaging the environment and threatening the health of our constituents. We must apply to those problems the sense of urgency which the report asks us to emphasize.
For instance, we have been working in my constituency with BCM Technologies for over a year to try to reach a complete solution to its chlorine emissions. We have found, despite commitments on the part of the company and on the part of the provincial Ministry of the Environment, that a year later the commitments have not been honoured. The air pollution continues and my constituents continue to experience health hazards and the lack of satisfactory environmental conditions which I think they have the right to expect as Canadians.
I want to talk about even more exciting topics, aside from air pollution, and to take a step down to what often seems to be the level of discussion in this Chamber. I want to talk about sewage and about garbage. When we talk about environmental problems, we must remember that there are sewage problems across the nation which we are not treating with urgency. One example is contained in a letter which I wrote in July, 1985 to the then Minister of the Environment, that is, the sewer system in south Windsor.
One might say that sewage is not something which reaches the levels of the high power rhetoric we have heard in the debate today, but fundamentally that is what the issue is all about. It is about ensuring that sewage systems in our communities are able to meet the needs of the people. We found in our community that our constant efforts to try to push the Government to accept the responsibility to provide assistance in the area of sewage systems have simply been rejected. We have seen this in the southern part of the City of Windsor and in the Township of Sandwich West. Recently a public meeting focused on this question.
We will be taken seriously as a country which cares about environmental issues when we start doing something about such mundane but serious problems as the antiquated sewer systems of our cities. As it stands at the moment, we simply let sewers run into international waters, with the result that rivers get polluted, again a potential health hazard, again a lack of the environmental protection which Canadians should expect in this country.
I have to say that it is just not sewage we have to talk about but garbage as well. For instance, the City of Detroit is planning to erect the largest incinerator in the United States without the latest technology to prevent the escape of material which will damage the air and be injurious to people's health which, it has been demonstrated in laboratory tests, will cause increases in cancer rates. We have to recognize that that kind
Supply
of problem is as crucial and urgent and is as serious as the concerns which have been indicated here.
I am impressed with this report. There are interesting and innovative ideas being suggested at the international level. I want to make the point that we in Canada, to prove our seriousness, have to start dealing with some of these mundane, down to earth problems of water pollution, air pollution, sewage and garbage. When we start doing that with the urgency and with the support of our people, then I think we will be taking the first steps to a safe environmental future for this country and for the world.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S O. 82- THE ENVIRONMENT- REQUEST THAT THE GOVERNMENT ENDORSE, ADOPT AND ADVOCATE, AT HOME AND ABROAD, THE GOALS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE BRUNDTLAND REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to speak to the motion moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia):
That this House urge the Government to endorse, adopt and advocate, at home and abroad, the goals and recommendations of the Report of the World Commission on Environment and Development (Brundtland Report), entitled "Our Common Future";
This Report, dealing with global concerns, challenges and endeavours, be adopted as the central policy of the federal Government, its agencies and commissions; and
That the Minister of the Environment advocate the spirit and the substance ol this Report at the coming General Assembly of the United Nations on behalf of Canadians and of the global community, thus continuing Canada's tradition of giving leadership on environmental matters.
Canada's leadership on the evolving world stage is becoming more and more important as we mature and become a respected nation in our second decade of development. Although perhaps not particularly relevant to the subject matter, I think in an ancillary way it is. 1 had the opportunity, it was a glorious one, to meet with Mr. Yehudi Menuhin today. In a conversation with him, he brought to my attention how important Canada has become on the world scene. He said that he found it particularly interesting that we, as Canadians, have developed culturally very distinctively. We have developed an artistic community with talents found almost nowhere else in the world where he has taught as a master. He equates that with the fact that we have in Canada a specific attitude, one of accepting the world as part of our responsibility, and that people who come here are welcomed and are encouraged to maintain their identity, their roots and to go back to their roots. He said, "It is not like teaching students from the Julliard School because they would not do what the students here do. Here they go back to their roots and the original interpretations. They have a sense of participation and belonging to past history which they bring with them and do not want to remove in any way. They want to maintain the links with the old and the new and they have pride in their heritage".
This brings me to the report which the World Commission on Environment and Development put together when it established this UN commission in December, 1983. This was strongly supported by Canada. We do have a very special role as a mature nation and as a partnership for the diverse beauty of this country as it is reflected by the people who are in it.

May 15, 1987
Supply
I would suggest that we listen very carefully to what has been written in this report by Dr. Brundtland, Norway's Prime Minister, and the 22 commissioners, two of whom are highly respected Canadians, namely, Maurice Strong and Jim MacNeill, who was the Secretary General for the commission. The report was released in London on April 27, 1987. This report is exciting because it is a positive one. It is not a doomsday report. It does not make you feel that the world is going to blow itself away, or that we are in inherent danger of disappearing as a race. This report lucidly advances the debate on the environment from a protection to a survival theme. It looks at the world in which we live to the global society and puts us all in this great big envelope. We do live together in an envelope. It might be trite to say that it is a global village, but, truly, Mr. Speaker, it is. What happens in other countries of the world impacts on us right here. There is no greater lesson than the Chernobyl affair which impacted on our reindeer herds, the caribou, milk and everything else. It is a reflection of something that happened seemingly so far away, and not too long ago it would have seemed very far away.
Looking at the prospects outlined in this report, it is important that the commissioners have placed the environment not in the context of just one public interest competing with others, but in the context of all our interests collectively, whether trade, health, the growth of our wheat or the development and concerns around acid rain. All of these economic activities and the fall-out from them impact upon our environment, which bring us to the very centre of economic activity and the pre-conditions that we have for the development of our world.
Each one of us has to live in our own community and one tends not to think of the larger world. We can ill afford that isolated view of society. We can ill afford to ignore our neighbours in this larger world.
The message is that we have to find a sustainable development process. 1 think all the forces of all the Ministries together here in Canada and around the world must put their heads and efforts together to ensure that our children and grandchildren and their children's children will have a world in which to live.
It is true that the document-for those who care to pick it up, and 1 would encourage people to do so-would seem to be very dry. It contains 348 pages, and 1 must admit that leafing through it I had to sort of push myself to find some of the areas of particular interest to me. It is, however, a vital and important document. It will be front and centre in the discussions to be held in the capitals and in the Parliaments around the world, no matter what the political bent of the Government in question. It will affect each and every one of us.
What is exciting about this report is that it is not a doomsday report. It offers new approaches and scenarios. It links the environment with what we do and how we live on a daily basis.
It indicates that there are unsolved problems and that there are no immediate answers, but it does offer some directions and ideas. It took three years, a lot of effort and a great deal of money to compile this report, and it has come up with some very positive facts which we would all do well to examine quite carefully.
The answer is not simple. It is not: "Stop the world, I want to get off'. The message is that there is room to grow in the world. We can make the economic ball roll. We like to call for jobs, jobs, jobs, but there are other ways of living without degrading the life around us. We do have the capacity to solve environmental problems.
I thought it was interesting that the report indicated that mass poverty could be overcome. I know that all of us have contributed to world hunger campaigns and have been sensitized through the mass media to the plight of starving people in the world.
The report tells us that there are absolutely no limits to our growth. The report actually links the problems of poverty in sub-Sahara Africa to the Chernobyl nuclear disaster and it links the deforestation of South America with acid rain in West Germany and here. It is fascinating that we think of each one of those as being separate entities. In reality, these crises are not separate. Environmental crises, developmental crises and energy crises are all one crisis that must be faced by each and every one of us. We must try to find a healthy and sustainable balance so we can live in this world. The fundamental question to be asked is how we are to find that sustainable balance.
We should listen to the report's call on world Governments, particularly those of the developed world, to think more broadly and deeply about environmental and developmental problems. It calls on us to think not just in terms of me, myself and I, not just in terms of instant gratification, and not just in terms of how I can climb the ladder, have more goods and services and be a bigger and fatter consumer. We must ask if we can live in society tomorrow. Will we be able to breathe, will society be here? This report says yes, if. That "if' is important.
The report suggests that we must use the intelligence that created the problems to resolve them. I think that is a modest enough aim and we should all try to devote our political will to making this world a place where we can live together.
I would like to deal with the interlocking crises. Until very recently, the world was a place where human activities and efforts were neatly compartmentalized by nations, by sectors such as energy, agriculture or trade, and by broad areas of concern, environmental, economic and social. All these concerns were related to cultural patterns that had evolved throughout the world and reflected common communal values which resulted from the choices and options taken by particular cultural entities. I suggest that most of these compartments have been dissolved and the world has become a global village.
I suggest as well that in these various global crises, there are
May 15, 1987

common public concerns. We began to recognize that just a short time ago.
I would suggest, and I do not think I am going beyond reality, that much of this recognition has to do with the feminine revolution. Women have become sensitive to the world and their environment. More particularly, the communications systems that now exist link us to the world within seconds. Women have been the nurturers of society and have begun to raise environmental concerns, nuclear concerns and survival concerns. I would salute the women's movement for having sensitized the world to this issue.
In Nairobi, a meeting of women was held at the end of the decade. Groups of women came from all corners of the world, from all socio-economic levels, and from every political Party imaginable. Some of the things that were said I found abominable and some of the things they did I found abhorrent. However, one common line ran through the entire debate and that was the volition on the part of women around the world to live in a better environment, a safe environment in which to bring up their children. That line transcended all ideologies and every sector, no matter what colour, race, creed, language or religion.
This report contains some very substantive facts and figures. It talks about the fact that the planet is going through a period of dramatic growth and fundamental change. It indicates that our world, which is presently made up of five billion people, must make room in a finite environment for another huge mass of humanity. The population will potentially level out at eight billion to 14 billion sometime within the next century. That is an awful lot of people.
It goes on to talk about the fact that economic activity has multiplied to create a world economy of $13 trillion. I cannot even imagine how many zeros there are in that figure. I am trying to indicate that these facts have to be translated into individual lives and individual survival. If we are to have economic activity that creates $13 trillion in the world economy and could grow five-fold to ten-fold in the coming half century, then I think we must develop the kind of survival policies that will allow us to consider the total environment, whether we are pulling raw materials from our forests, our soils, our seas or our waterways.
People are the ultimate resource. Improvements in education, health and nutrition allow people to better use the resources they command and to stretch them even further. The concern for the population problem is underlined in this report, and if one reads it carefully, one sees that there is a sense of hope that there could be human equality if we would simply sit down long enough to develop common policies to live together.
One additional person in an industrial country consumes far more and places far more pressure on natural resources than one additional person in the Third World. Consumption patterns and preferences are as important as numbers of consumers in the conservation of our resources.
Supply
What about environment and development? Population growth and development are linked in very complex ways. In the past, the intensification of agriculture and the production of higher yields helped nations cope with increasing populations and pressures on available land. However, that is not the case today. Today there is over-production, yet there are starving people. There must be something wrong with our international policies. It seems to me that if we could find a way to balance our agricultural policies so that the starving people had food and we, overstuffed people, did not waste food, we could find a solution to some of the problems to which I have been referring.
We are facing rapid technological change. It is important that the commission has made some positive recommendations. It has recommended alternatives to allow us to continue to live with a decent life-style throughout the world. The commission talks about sustainable economic development and growth. It directs us on how to think and act in order to make life sustainable. We must look at new ways of living if we wish to survive as a species. As you and I know, our resources are not infinite. Whatever we do, we must think on the larger world scale as we all impact on each other in this world.
The population increases to which I referred earlier bring a series of additional concerns for social and economic development. This has created the problem of unmanageable cities which we must be seriously concerned with. A concern for population growth is part of the broader concern for the rapid rate of economic and social development in developing countries. We cannot afford to be selfish. We must think about education, growth, and development for all the world's children. As we think of our brothers and sisters around the world we must think of what will make life liveable for them. A balance must be established between population size and available resources.
We must find ways to make sustainable human progress a reality. This report has been able to do this. We need policies which will enable us to control our enormous population growth and enable people to have choices. We need improved public health and child nutrition. Family planning services must be further developed and integrated with other health programs such as mother and child care programs, preschool education, and education in general.
We need a commitment to rural development. We cannot empty the countryside, make vast parklands, and put everyone into huge cosmopolitan centres. We must develop policies which will allow people to grow and develop in their own areas. Canada has a good model which has partially worked within our regional development projects. Perhaps we can share with others and learn so that we do not depopulate the countryside, so that we find a better pattern of development for the entire world.
We must find a way to spread employment opportunities throughout the nations. Not every nation can be a producer

May 15, 1987
Supply
with no nation being consumers of the products of others. That will not work. We must determine how to control and develop our cities and encourage people to stay in their natural environment without feeling that they do not have an adequate chance in life.
1 talked about the need to improve health. This is absolutely fundamental in the developing world. The problems are critical. The concerns for ill health are closely related to environmental conditions and developmental problems. There is inadequacy of water supply and sanitation, which are direct causes of widespread and debilitating diseases such as diarrhea and various worm infestations.
Clean water is not accessible to 1.7 billion people, and 1.2 billion do not have adequate sanitation. If we could solve that problem alone many diseases would be controlled and life would be more liveable for many people. Canada is doing very good work throughout the world with some of our programs. Other nations must do the same.
1 know that my time is running out. 1 would like to urge strongly that through the United Nations we find some way to answer the questions raised. There is a sunset clause of December 31 in this report. The United Nations Secretariat must find a way to implement this document by then. We do not want it to gather dust. There is an urgency for everyone in the world. We should support the call of the United Nations Secretary General to constitute, under his chairmanship, a special United Nations board extending to all the nations of the world.
If we really believe that we have a common future we should consider the words of the poet, Bliss Carmen, who said that we are moulded by the conditions and surroundings in which we live, but we often forget that the environment is largely what we make it. I hope that we will be considerate and make it liveable for all.
