subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S O. 82- THE ENVIRONMENT- REQUEST THAT THE GOVERNMENT ENDORSE, ADOPT AND ADVOCATE, AT HOME AND ABROAD, THE GOALS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE BRUNDTLAND REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on the motion of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) with regard to the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development, the Brundtland report entitled, Our Common Future. I would like to congratulate the Member for raising this issue today. I recognize his genuine interest in environmental concerns. We on this side of the House sometimes tend to heckle him in a partisan way a little bit unfairly. While he may not have been as effective as the present Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) when he held that important job, it was not due to any lack of sincerity or genuine interest in the issues on his part.
As a member of the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology I would like to add a few comments to those which have already been made this afternoon. Canadian technology can play a significant role in achieving the objectives set out in Our Common Future. I hope 1 will have time to talk a little about that toward the end of my speech.
The report on the World Commission on Environment and Development recommends that new mechanisms be established to ensure that, as a matter of routine, environmental consequences be considered when economic decisions are made.
The report was presented at the beginning of the second meeting of the National Task Force on Environment and Economy. This task force, in itself, is an innovative response to the Brundtland Report in that it brings together the federal, provincial, public and private sector to improve co-ordination of economic decision-making in Canada.
The Minister of the Environment, upon receipt of the report, pointed out: "As the thinking which went into the establishment of this task force illustrates, better integration of environmental considerations into economic planning and decision-making is and has been a priority direction set by this Government".
1 am pleased and encouraged that the importance which the Government attaches to the integration of environmental and economic decision-making has been taken up as a major thrust of the Brundtland report. The report is both timely and appropriate, and fully in keeping with the priorities of the Government.
The report dramatically underscores the need to make the leap from focusing our environmental efforts on dealing after the fact with the adverse impact of economic development, to starting, instead, to concern ourselves more with economic
May 15, 1987

strategies and developments which are environmentally sound and sustainable in the first instance.
The fact is that the environment and the economy are not two distinct entities. They are not two solitudes. They are interrelated and indivisible. In fact, they are the two sides of the same coin.
The commission was composed of 22 eminent people, most of them politicians from around the world. The Prime Minister of Norway, Gro Brundtland, formerly her country's Environment Minister, headed the group. I want to emphasize again that the majority of these investigators were, like us, politicians. They were not theoreticians, academics, or ecological ideologues, but people experienced in identifying practical responses to actual problems. What their report makes clear is that our planet's survival is at stake and that only concerted international action undertaken now can save it. In effect, either the buck stops here or the world does.
That message confirms what scientists have been saying for some time now, that the human race is progressively eliminating, through environmental mismanagement, its own chances of a future. Pollution has become so widespread, so varied, and so pervasive that no corner of the earth is free from it. Nations are threatened, not just by their own sources of contamination, but also by those of their neighbours and by those of countries half a world away. Sulphur dioxide rises from smokestacks in northeastern United States and falls as acid rain here in eastern Ontario, killing our trees and lakes. Nuclear fall-out drifts westward from Chernobyl over northern Europe and the Arctic, polluting crops and livestock. The indiscriminate use of chlorofluorocarbons, CFCs, in the developed world is thinning the stratospheric layer of ozone that blankets the earth from the sun's ultraviolet rays. In the process, millions of people around the globe are being exposed to an increased risk of cancer. The problem is contributing to a greenhouse effect that may eventually reduce Canada's rich prairie grain belt to a desert and cause floods in Atlantic Canada.
Pollution respects no state boundaries or political divisions. It carries no national passport or corporate key. That fact is inescapable as well as dismaying. It also, however, points us toward the approach we must take in the face of such an enemy. In our present situation, it makes no sense to argue unduly about jurisdictions and responsibilities. We are all part of the human family, the global village. We must, therefore, co-operate willingly, energetically and immediately if we are to preserve our world.
It is not a question of saving developed nations at the expense of the Third World, or of cleaning up North America without regard to Europe or the USSR. We are all in this together; and, as that old saying goes, if we do not hang together, we shall all hang separately. Those are our options, plain and simple.
The Brundtland Report makes the point clearly that: "These are not separate crises, an environmental crisis, a development crisis, an energy crisis. They are all one".
Supply
Economies depend, for their survival, on the resource bases supplied by a healthy environment. The environment depends, for its survival, on economic decision-making that takes full account of impacts on resources. Any society that ignores that equation does so at its peril.
The implications of the link between the environment and the economy are far-reaching and complex.
Canada is, after all, perhaps the pre-eminent candidate to take the lead in helping meet the needs that arise around the globe from environmental requirements. The solutions we find to soil erosion on the Prairies, the equipment we develop to curb pollution, the methods we devise to preserve our fragile northern tundra or our West Coast rain forests, all can be crucial not only to our nation's future but to the future of the world as well.
Solutions that work for industries in Canada can be applied with the necessary modifications, and with equal success, to industries in Indonesia, Brazil or Zambia, and to industries in Germany's Rhur Valley, in Rotterdam or Yokohama. Our nation-the nation that developed the first geo-stationary communications satellite and the space arm, that built the Bluenose and spanned a continent with rail lines-can meet the environmental challenge.
We would urge that the report of the Brundtland Commission be taken up by all United Nations member countries, and that the recommendations be considered as well at the national level.
Needless to say, Canada, as a long-term supporter of the United Nations, expects to play an active role in the debate of this report in the United Nations this fall. I look forward to that debate and to Canada's leadership role in it.
In the few minutes remaining, I would like to read a very short excerpt from Our Common Future, the report we are discussing this afternoon, just to emphasize the urgency of the issues that this report raises. It states:
The World Commission on Environment and Development first met in October 1984, and published its report 900 days later, in April 1987. Over those few days:
The drought-triggered, environment-development crisis in Africa peaked, putting 35 million people at risk, killing perhaps a million.
A leak from a pesticides factory in Bhopal, India, killed more than 2,000 people and blinded and injured over 200,000 more.
Liquid gas tanks exploded in Mexico City, killing 1,000 and leaving thousands more homeless.
The Chernobyl nuclear reactor explosion sent nuclear fall-out across Europe, increasing the risks of future human cancers.
Agricultural chemicals, solvents, and mercury flowed into the Rhine River during a warehouse fire in Switzerland, killing millions of fish and threatening drinking water in the Federal Republic of Germany and the Netherlands.
An estimated 60 million died of diarrhoeal diseases related to unsafe drinking water and malnutrition; most of the victims were children.
At the outset of my remarks, I mentioned that I believe that Canadian technology can play a role. I also described some of the high technology that we have developed in Canada that can be applied throughout the world.

May 15, 1987
Supply
We should not think only in terms of high-tech. We can do so much simply by funding small clean water projects in the Third World. 1 refer to the 60 million deaths in a period of less than three years from diarrhoea caused by unsafe drinking water. It seems to me that clean water is the key to economic and social development in Africa and Asia. The Government is doing a lot. In particular, I congratulate CIDA and the private sector non-governmental organizations in this country which are doing so much to try to provide clean water in Africa and Asia. I urge the Government however, to do much more. If we were just to concentrate on this one way of helping our fellow citizens in the rest of the world, it would go a long way towards achieving the objectives of this report.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S O. 82- THE ENVIRONMENT- REQUEST THAT THE GOVERNMENT ENDORSE, ADOPT AND ADVOCATE, AT HOME AND ABROAD, THE GOALS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE BRUNDTLAND REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise this afternoon on the motion introduced in accordance with Standing Order 82(12) of the House of Commons and sponsored today by my colleague the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). In my view, this is an extremely important motion which gives us as parliamentarians an opportunity to consider environmental problems, and more especially the Brundtland Report which has just been made public.
I am very proud to see that my colleague, the former Minister of the Environment in the Liberal Cabinet, has brought to the attention of the House this report drafted under the auspices of the United Nations. I am very proud of his initiative because it shows to what extent an individual can, after being a Cabinet Minister, continue to be deeply interested in this issue.
In a number of cases the Environment was a first department for several Ministers and a stage in their career. I have no hesitation in saying that, of all the Ministers of the Environment I have known since the department was established, my colleague from Davenport is propably the Minister who has shown the most interest, the most conviction in his work, and the greatest desire to promote the environmental cause. This is why I hope that in the near future he will be given the opportunity to become Minister of the Environment again so as to continue the work which he began with such dedication in his department and which, unfortunately, has not been followed up as closely since he left.
There is no doubt that the ongoing discussions with the Americans are not producing the results which he would hope to see. With respect to environmental matters the American authorities should indeed act much more responsibly and take positive measures to reduce the pollution we are getting from the United States instead of being satisfied with yet more studies.
I spoke recently to Quebec farmers who described how much sugar bushes are threatened by acid rain, how much an industry that is truly close to home, truly of Quebec, truly Canadian-the maple sugar and maple syrup industry-is seriously threatened by acid rain and the inaction of numerous corporations that pollute our environment. Whether they are
Canadian or American, this is a major problem to be addressed.
There is no doubt that as we receive that report prepared by the United Nations, we must view it as a very important document. It is my conviction that the Brundtland Report is no doubt the single most important environmental document of the decade. What one finds encouraging when making a quick study of the main recommendations of this report is that here is a practical report, a report that is filled with concrete proposals. It is essential that those proposals be accepted and implemented by the most industrialized nations in the world.
The efforts to protect our environment must come first and foremost from the richer countries of this planet. Clearly, we cannot expect developing nations, the poorer nations to assume the responsibility for depolluting our environment, depolluting the world, if the richer nations, first the United States and second Canada and the other industrialized nations, do not do their share.
1 hope that the Government of Canada will review this document very closely and will respond to it. At any rate, the resolution put forward by our colleague for Davenport is very clear in that regard. It not only suggests but urges the Government to act upont it. 1 quote:
should
-this House urge the Government to endorse, adopt and advocate, at home and abroad, the goals and recommendations of the Report of the World Commission on Environment and Development (Brundtland Report), "Our Common Future"; That this Report, dealing with global concerns, challenges and endeavours, be adopted as the central policy of the federal Government, its agencies and commissions;

And finally, it is clear the Minister of Environment (Mr. McMillan) should ensure that at the next United Nations General Assembly, the promotion of the spirit and substance of that United Nations report, on behalf of Canadians and the world community, be in line with the Canadian tradition of leadership in the area of environment.
It is therefore clear that we expect concrete steps, not merely fine speeches but concrete steps from the Canadian Government when it makes decisions concerning the protection of our environment.
I represent a constituency that is located in Montreal, an island in the middle of the St. Lawrence River, one of the most beautiful rivers in the world, but also one of the most polluted unfortunately. Efforts have to be made by the federal as well as provincial authorities and by the private sector not only to control that pollution, but also to take radical steps to clean up that pollution. I do hope that in a near future, in the Montreal area, it will be possible as it used to be possible some years ago, a few decades ago, to swim in the St. Lawrence River without taking any risks and to fully enjoy this magnificent river which is one of the most majestic in the world, to enjoy the beaches
May 15, 1987

and the waters of that river which we have unfortunately ignored too much.
In conclusion, may I suggest that it is essential that government authorities throughout the world think about these words of hope which were spoken by the chairwoman of that committee, Mrs. Brundtland, and I quote:
"Our report-is not a prediction of ever-increasing environmental decay, poverty and hardship in an ever-more polluted world among ever-decreasing resources-
"We see instead the possibility for a new era of economic growth-absolutely essential to relieve the great poverty that is deepening in much of the developing world."
The panel which she chaired and on which sat an important and well known Canadian, Mr. Maurice Strong, considered population growth, energy strategies, global warming because of atmospheric changes, man-made disasters and economic conditions that cause the destruction of tropical forests. "Poverty itself pollutes the environment," the panel said. It stated further:
"Those who are poor and hungry will often destroy their immediate environment in order to survive: they will cut down forests; their livestock will overgraze grasslands; they will overuse marginal land and in growing numbers they will crowd into congested cities.
In order to live in a better world it is absolutely important that the leaders of the world get together not only to fight pollution but, in the process of fighting pollution, to establish new programs for this era of economic growth in order to spread the growth among all the nations of the world. The rich nations of the world must help the poor nations of the world to tackle the problems with which they are confronted.

It is on this note that I wish to end my remarks, by saying that I welcome wholeheartedly the motion introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). Through his initiative, we have been given a deeper awareness of that important document published by the United Nations, and I hope the Conservative Government will not abdicate its responsibilities and will take quick action on this matter.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S O. 82- THE ENVIRONMENT- REQUEST THAT THE GOVERNMENT ENDORSE, ADOPT AND ADVOCATE, AT HOME AND ABROAD, THE GOALS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE BRUNDTLAND REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to rise in the closing moments of this debate to offer some comments. Today has been a great opportunity for all Hon. Members to address the problem at hand, and I note the commonality of the objective. I feel that Members from all Parties have expressed their deep concern with respect to the quality of the environment and what we must do as Canadians to put it into perspective.
The opening chapters of the Brundtland report suggest that a first step toward addressing common environmental concerns is the recognition that most of the problems of ecology and economy that, until now, have been dealt with separately, are in fact very closely linked together and require integrated action on a global scale. Our Government is particularly encouraged that the report stresses the need for more coordination between economic and environmental development. The report reaffirms that we must make the leap from preoccupation with undoing environmental damage to planning and managing our affairs so that economic development efforts are environmentally sound and sustainable in the first place.
The National Task Force on the Economy and the Environment which was set up last year is an excellent example of how we can do this. An encouraging aspect to me is the recognition that we have the technology, the know-how, the ability to address the global problems with which we are confronted. The challenge with which we are confronted is: Do we have the will to do it? That is our collective challenge as parliamentarians.
The report shows that Canadian concerns about acid rain, soil and water degradation, toxic waste, the holes in our ozone layer and ozone depletion, and sustainable use of our natural resources are environmental and economic issues of the highest order both in Canada and world-wide. We are involved with this in Canada, as much as the rest of the world is involved, in the sense that our children and our grandchildren will be dramatically affected by it as much as anyone. I recall hearing just a few days ago how a change in our mean temperature of only two degrees could precipitate another ice-age. Just think how catastrophic that would be in terms of our ability to produce food and to continue to exist on earth.

At the moment in China alone the citizens of that country are burning annually more than one cubic mile of coal. Let us think about what that is doing to our atmosphere and the possibility of the climatic change it can precipitate. Around the world annually we produce about one cubic mile of solid garbage of which we have to dispose. The problems we face are enormous.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) will be discussing the report which we have been talking about today with his colleagues and with all parliamentarians. Following these discussions, and after hearing from non-governmental organizations and others, a formal and detailed governmental response to the recommendations of the commission will be
announced. Thereafter Canada has every intention to participate in the debate which will take place at the General Assembly of the United Nations this fall. When that happens I am confident that all Canadians will be proud.
